title: Linear-size labeled sample compression
open: Does every binary concept class of VC dimension \(d\) admit a labeled sample-compression scheme of size \(O(d)\), independent of the original sample size?
status: Originates with Littlestone and Warmuth in 1986. General schemes of size exponential in \(d\) are known; the linear bound remains open.
why: It would give a universal explanation of learnability through small reconstructible certificates.
key_works: Littlestone and Warmuth (1986), *Relating Data Compression and Learnability*; Moran and Yehudayoff (2016), *Sample Compression Schemes for VC Classes*, arXiv:1503.06960; Attias et al. (2025), *Sample Compression Scheme Reductions*, arXiv:2410.13012.

title: Linear-size unlabeled compression
open: Does every binary VC class admit an unlabeled compression scheme of size \(O(d)\), without storing the selected examples’ labels?
status: The stronger conjecture that size \(d\) always suffices is false. Pálvölgyi and Tardos constructed counterexamples; these do not settle a universal linear bound.
why: It separates information carried by example selection from information explicitly carried by labels.
key_works: Kuzmin and Warmuth (2007), *Unlabeled Compression Schemes for Maximum Classes*; Pálvölgyi and Tardos (2021 version), *Unlabeled Compression Schemes Exceeding the VC-dimension*, arXiv:1811.12471.

title: Polynomial exact compression for agnostic absolute-loss regression
open: Does every real-valued function class of finite pseudo-dimension admit an exact agnostic compression scheme whose size is polynomial in that dimension under absolute loss?
status: Explicitly posed in 2024. Bounded approximate schemes are available, but the general exact polynomial-size statement remains a separate question.
why: It would turn noisy regression solutions into small, loss-preserving training certificates.
key_works: Attias, Hanneke, Kontorovich, and Sadigurschi (2024), *Agnostic Sample Compression Schemes for Regression*, PMLR 235:2069–2085.

title: Polynomial fat-dimension compression for squared-loss regression
open: Under squared loss, can approximate agnostic compression always have size polynomial in the appropriate scale-dependent fat-shattering dimension and accuracy parameters?
status: Explicit 2024 question. Generic constructions have exponential dimension dependence; linear regression admits substantially smaller schemes.
why: It would connect real-valued learnability to practically useful dataset reduction.
key_works: Attias et al. (2024), *Agnostic Sample Compression Schemes for Regression*; Attias et al. (2025), *Sample Compression Scheme Reductions*, arXiv:2410.13012.

title: Linear recursive teaching dimension
open: Is the recursive teaching dimension of every finite binary concept class \(O(d)\), where \(d\) is its VC dimension?
status: Studied since the early 2010s and explicitly posed at COLT 2015. A general \(O(d^2)\) upper bound is known; some classes require more than \(d\).
why: It asks whether concepts learnable from few random examples are always teachable with comparably few carefully chosen examples.
key_works: Doliwa et al. (2014), *Recursive Teaching Dimension, VC-Dimension and Sample Compression*; Simon and Zilles (2015), *Open Problem: Recursive Teaching Dimension Versus VC Dimension*; Hu et al. (2017), *Quadratic Upper Bound for Recursive Teaching Dimension of Finite VC Classes*, arXiv:1702.05677.

title: Local regularization for all PAC-learnable multiclass classes
open: Can every PAC-learnable multiclass class be learned by selecting sample-consistent hypotheses using a regularizer depending on the hypothesis and test point?
status: Posed in 2024. The analogous transductive statement was disproved in 2025; the cited negative result explicitly leaves the PAC question open.
why: It tests whether regularization can remain a universal organizing principle beyond binary classification.
key_works: Asilis et al. (2024), *Open Problem: Can Local Regularization Learn All Multiclass Problems?*; Jafar, Asilis, and Dughmi (2025), *Local Regularizers Are Not Transductive Learners*, arXiv:2502.07187.

title: Structural characterization of agnostic direct-sum risk
open: Identify structural invariants that determine the agnostic learning rate of \(r\)-fold direct sums under whole-vector zero–one loss.
status: The 2024 question cannot be answered from the base class’s minimax rate alone: a 2026 separation gives classes with identical base rates but different direct-sum rates.
why: It would predict the statistical cost of learning several outputs jointly rather than independently.
key_works: Hanneke, Moran, and Waknine (2024), *Open Problem: Direct Sums in Learning Theory*; More, Das, and Gupta (2026), *A Rate Separation for Agnostic Direct Sums*, arXiv:2608.06951.

title: Exact list-length composition
open: Determine the minimum list size needed to learn a product class from the minimum list sizes of its factors, including when the known upper and lower composition bounds are attained.
status: Explicit in the 2024 direct-sums program. Bounds involving products of the factor list sizes leave a nontrivial gap.
why: It quantifies how prediction ambiguity compounds in structured outputs.
key_works: Hanneke, Moran, and Waknine (2024), *Open Problem: Direct Sums in Learning Theory*; Charikar and Pabbaraju (2023), *A Characterization of List Learnability*.

title: DS-dimension product laws
open: Obtain sharp formulas or necessary-and-sufficient structural bounds for the DS dimension of products of multiclass hypothesis classes.
status: Product behavior was highlighted in 2024. The 2026 resolution of optimal dependence on DS dimension makes its algebra under composition more consequential, not automatically settled.
why: Such laws would let one derive structured-prediction sample complexity from reusable components.
key_works: Hanneke et al. (2024), *Open Problem: Direct Sums in Learning Theory*; Pabbaraju (2026), *The Optimal Sample Complexity of Multiclass and List Learning*, arXiv:2604.24749.

title: Quantitative uniform estimation on product spaces
open: Determine sharp sample complexity in linear VC dimension, number of coordinates, accuracy, and the distribution’s departure from independence for uniform estimation on product spaces.
status: A 2026 theorem characterizes qualitative estimability under absolute continuity relative to the product of marginals. Quantitative bounds are explicitly left for further work.
why: It could make statistically tractable classes with infinite ordinary VC dimension usable.
key_works: Holzman, Moran, and Shlimovich (2026), *Uniform Laws of Large Numbers in Product Spaces*, arXiv:2603.24493.

title: Computational characterization beyond DS dimension
open: Characterize which multiclass classes with finite DS dimension admit polynomial-time learning under explicit representation and optimization-oracle assumptions.
status: Research target. Statistical characterization and optimal dimension dependence have advanced through 2026; they do not themselves provide efficient implementations for arbitrary represented classes.
why: It separates existence of a learner from implementable multiclass learning.
key_works: Brukhim et al. (2022), *A Characterization of Multiclass Learnability*, DOI:10.1109/FOCS54457.2022.00093; Pabbaraju (2026), *The Optimal Sample Complexity of Multiclass and List Learning*, arXiv:2604.24749.

title: Characterizing compressible list-learnable classes
open: Find a structural characterization of list-learnable classes that admit bounded sample compression, including the roles of permitted output-list size and compression reconstruction.
status: A blanket list analogue of the compression conjecture is false: even three-label, two-list-learnable examples can fail to be compressible.
why: It would identify exactly which ambiguous prediction problems support finite training certificates.
key_works: Hanneke, Moran, and Waknine (2026 version), *List Sample Compression and Uniform Convergence*, arXiv:2403.10889.

title: Polynomial-time uniform-distribution DNF learning
open: Learn arbitrary polynomial-size DNF formulas from random labeled examples under the uniform Boolean distribution in polynomial time, without membership queries.
status: A longstanding problem from the early PAC-learning era. Restricted DNF families and stronger access models admit better algorithms; the general random-example target remains unresolved.
why: It is a central test of whether simple Boolean representations are computationally learnable.
key_works: Klivans and Servedio (2001), work on subexponential DNF learning, DOI:10.1145/380752.380809; Lecomte and Tan (2021), *Sharper Bounds on the Fourier Concentration of DNFs*, arXiv:2109.04525.

title: Distribution-free DNF learning with membership queries
open: Is there a polynomial-time PAC learner for polynomial-size DNF under arbitrary input distributions when membership queries are allowed?
status: Longstanding. Recent locally mixing random-walk methods improve the algorithmic landscape but do not establish the general polynomial-time target.
why: It isolates whether active access to labels overcomes the computational difficulty of distribution-free DNF learning.
key_works: Alman, Nadimpalli, Patel, and Servedio (2025), *DNF Learning via Locally Mixing Random Walks*.

title: Fixed-parameter tractable learning of juntas
open: Learn an arbitrary \(k\)-junta from uniform random examples in time \(\operatorname{poly}(n,2^k,1/\epsilon)\), rather than \(n^{\Omega(k)}\)-type search.
status: Studied for more than two decades. Algorithms exploit influence, Fourier structure, or restrictions on the junta; the unrestricted parameter dependence remains the central target.
why: It would efficiently discover a small unknown relevant feature set without favorable signal assumptions.
key_works: Mossel, O’Donnell, and Servedio (2003), *Learning Juntas*, DOI:10.1145/780542.780574; their subsequent work on learning functions of \(k\) relevant variables.

title: Polynomial-time learning parity with noise
open: Recover or predict an unknown parity on \(n\) bits from uniform examples whose labels have independent constant-rate noise in polynomial time, or establish hardness from a standard complexity assumption.
status: Open for decades. Subexponential algorithms and numerous parameter-specific improvements exist; general polynomial-time learning would undermine widely used LPN hardness assumptions.
why: It is both a basic noisy-learning problem and a foundation for lightweight cryptography.
key_works: Blum, Kalai, and Wasserman (2003), *Noise-tolerant Learning, the Parity Problem, and the Statistical Query Model*; Golowich et al. (2024), *On Learning Parities with Dependent Noise*, arXiv:2404.11325.

title: Mansour’s conjecture
open: Prove that every size-\(s\) DNF has all but \(\epsilon\) of its Fourier mass supported on \(s^{O_\epsilon(1)}\) coefficients; the stronger customary formulation specifies \(s^{O(\log(1/\epsilon))}\).
status: Originates in the 1990s. General quasi-polynomial concentration bounds and stronger results for restricted or random DNFs are known.
why: It would yield efficient Fourier-based learning and explain the spectral simplicity of DNF formulas.
key_works: Mansour’s 1990s Fourier-concentration work; Klivans, Lee, and Wan (2010), *Mansour’s Conjecture Is True for Random DNF Formulas*; Lecomte and Tan (2021), *Sharper Bounds on the Fourier Concentration of DNFs*, arXiv:2109.04525.

title: Fourier entropy–influence conjecture
open: Does every Boolean function satisfy \(H(\widehat f^2)\le C\,I(f)\) for a universal constant \(C\)?
status: Friedgut–Kalai conjecture from 1996. Many structured classes and weaker general inequalities are known; 2026 work supplies further evidence rather than a general proof.
why: It would tightly connect sensitivity to spectral description length, with consequences for learning low-influence functions.
key_works: O’Donnell and Tan (2013), *A Composition Theorem for the Fourier Entropy-Influence Conjecture*; Han (2025), *A New Bound for the Fourier-Entropy-Influence Conjecture*, arXiv:2312.08271; González, MacManus, and Pereyra (2026), *Further Evidence Towards the Fourier Entropy-Influence Conjecture*, arXiv:2606.00246.

title: Distribution-independent SQ learning versus linear dimension
open: Does efficient distribution-independent statistical-query learning imply low dimension complexity: an appropriately small linear feature representation with comparable learning guarantees?
status: Explicit COLT 2026 open problem.
why: A positive answer would sharply restrict the distribution-independent advantage of nonlinear learning.
key_works: Feldman, Kamath, and Srebro (2026), *Invited Open Problem: Is the Power of Deep Learning over Linear Models Inherently Distribution Dependent?*, PMLR 336:7117–7122.

title: Distribution-independent neural SGD versus linear learning
open: If a benign neural architecture can be learned by gradient descent or SGD under every input distribution, must an appropriately efficient linear-model learner also exist?
status: Explicit 2026 question, distinct from the SQ formulation because standard SGD need not behave like an arbitrary SQ algorithm.
why: It would locate the source of deep learning’s advantages in architecture, optimization, or distributional structure.
key_works: Feldman, Kamath, and Srebro (2026), *Is the Power of Deep Learning over Linear Models Inherently Distribution Dependent?*; Barzilai and Shamir (2026), *Limitations of SGD for Multi-Index Models Beyond Statistical Queries*.

title: Planted clique below the square-root scale
open: Find a randomized polynomial-time algorithm that reliably detects or recovers a planted clique of size \(n^{1/2-\delta}\), for fixed \(\delta>0\), or justify its impossibility under a standard assumption.
status: Open for decades. Strong lower bounds apply to restricted algorithmic families, including bounded-degree sum-of-squares, not all polynomial-time algorithms.
why: Planted-clique hardness supports many proposed computational barriers in statistics and learning.
key_works: Barak et al. (2016), *A Nearly Tight Sum-of-Squares Lower Bound for the Planted Clique Problem*, arXiv:1604.03084; Kunisky, Wein, and Bandeira (2019), *Notes on Computational Hardness of Hypothesis Testing*, arXiv:1907.11636.

title: Sharp polynomial-time sparse-PCA phase diagram
open: Determine the exact computational thresholds for detection and recovery in sparse spiked covariance models across sparsity, dimension, sample size, and signal strength.
status: Conditional reductions and restricted-model lower bounds establish substantial gaps, but a complete algorithmic phase diagram is not established.
why: It would distinguish insufficient data from insufficient computation in sparse latent-factor discovery.
key_works: Berthet and Rigollet (2013), *Computational Lower Bounds for Sparse PCA*, arXiv:1304.0828; Kunisky et al. (2019), *Notes on Computational Hardness of Hypothesis Testing*, arXiv:1907.11636.

title: Computational threshold for spiked tensor recovery
open: Determine whether polynomial-time algorithms can recover a rank-one signal in Gaussian tensor noise at signal strengths substantially below known spectral and iterative thresholds.
status: The statistical–computational separation has been investigated since 2014. Information-theoretic thresholds and limitations of several algorithmic families are much better understood than unrestricted computation.
why: Tensor methods appear in latent-variable estimation, higher-order statistics, and learning nonlinear features.
key_works: Montanari and Richard (2014), *A Statistical Model for Tensor PCA*, arXiv:1411.1076; Jagannath and collaborators (2020), *Statistical Thresholds for Tensor PCA*, DOI:10.1214/19-AAP1547.

title: When low-degree failure predicts all efficient algorithms
open: State and prove a broadly applicable, nonvacuous theorem connecting low-degree polynomial failure to computational hardness for a precisely delimited family of planted inference models.
status: Research target. Low-degree analysis successfully predicts many thresholds, but it is not an unconditional characterization of all efficient inference.
why: It would convert a powerful diagnostic into a reliable foundation for computational lower bounds.
key_works: Kunisky, Wein, and Bandeira (2019), *Notes on Computational Hardness of Hypothesis Testing: Predictions Using the Low-Degree Likelihood Ratio*, arXiv:1907.11636.

title: Many-community SBM algorithms in the remaining density regimes
open: For stochastic block models with \(K\ge\sqrt n\), achieve the conjectured efficient recovery threshold throughout graph-density regimes not covered by existing matching algorithms.
status: In 2026, low-degree lower bounds cover all densities, while matching polynomial-time algorithms cover sparse and moderately sparse regimes.
why: It would clarify when many small communities can be recovered efficiently rather than treating the classical fixed-\(K\) threshold as universal.
key_works: Carpentier, Giraud, and Verzelen (2026), *Phase Transition for Stochastic Block Model with More than \(\sqrt n\) Communities*, PMLR 336:938–1000.

title: Efficient graph alignment beyond convex-relaxation thresholds
open: Determine the polynomial-time recovery threshold for correlated Gaussian graph alignment, beyond the noise regime where standard doubly stochastic or hypercube relaxations succeed.
status: A 2026 analysis locates those relaxations’ transition near \(n^{-1/2}\), up to logarithmic factors. This is not a threshold for all efficient algorithms.
why: It would improve matching of noisy networks, relational datasets, and latent correspondences.
key_works: Massoulié, Varma, Vassaux, and Waldspurger (2026), *Phase Transition in Convex Relaxations for Graph Alignment*, PMLR 336:4999–5020.

title: Generic complex phase retrieval below \(4M-4\) measurements
open: For generic complex measurements with \(N=4M-5\), determine the probability of injective phase retrieval and its asymptotic behavior as \(M\) grows.
status: The old universal necessity of \(4M-4\) measurements is false. A refined 2025 open-problem formulation asks about the probability and asymptotics of exceptional injective configurations.
why: It would sharpen identifiability limits for phaseless sensing and latent inverse problems.
key_works: Bandeira et al. (2026), *Randomstrasse101: Open Problems of 2025*, arXiv:2603.29571, discussing the refined Vinzant phase-retrieval questions.

title: Tensor type-2 inequalities in the remaining norm regime
open: Prove or refute the proposed type-2 bound for Gaussian series of order-\(r\) tensors in injective \(\ell_p\) norms in the remaining range \(2\le p<2r\).
status: Explicitly catalogued in the 2025 Randomstrasse problems. The corresponding regime \(p\ge2r\) has supporting results.
why: Such inequalities control random tensor fluctuations underlying estimation and high-order learning methods.
key_works: Bandeira et al. (2026), *Randomstrasse101: Open Problems of 2025*, arXiv:2603.29571.

title: Constant-factor instance-optimal identity testing
open: Give a concise functional \(\Phi(q,\epsilon)\) characterizing, within universal constant factors, the samples needed to distinguish \(p=q\) from \(\mathrm{TV}(p,q)>\epsilon\).
status: Explicit COLT 2024 problem. Existing characterizations involve differently truncated norms whose bounds need not agree within constants.
why: It would tell an experimenter how difficult a specific goodness-of-fit problem actually is.
key_works: Valiant and Valiant (2014), *An Automatic Inequality Prover and Instance Optimal Identity Testing*; Canonne (2024), *Open Problem: Tight Characterization of Instance-Optimal Identity Testing*.

title: Exact logarithmic factors in discrete conditional-independence testing
open: Remove unnecessary polylogarithmic factors, or prove them necessary, in discrete conditional-independence testing across alphabet-size and accuracy regimes.
status: The principal polynomial sample-complexity gaps for both \(\ell_1\) and KL formulations were closed in 2026. The sharper target is beyond that up-to-polylogarithms resolution.
why: Logarithmic factors can dominate tests with many conditioning categories.
key_works: Seyfried, Mishra, Sen, and Tomamichel (2026), *Optimal Sample Complexity Lower Bounds on Conditional Independence Testing*, PMLR 336:5828–5873.

title: Adaptive conditional-independence testing under unknown smoothness
open: Under an explicit nonparametric smoothness model, determine the unavoidable adaptation penalty when smoothness and effective conditioning dimension are unknown.
status: Research target. Unrestricted distribution-free conditional-independence testing is already impossible; the question concerns restricted, testable model families.
why: Causal and graphical-model procedures rarely know the regularity parameters assumed by their tests.
key_works: Shah and Peters (2020), *The Hardness of Conditional Independence Testing and the Generalised Covariance Measure*, arXiv:1804.07203.

title: Robust regression’s full sample–condition-number–runtime frontier
open: For contaminated Gaussian-design regression with unknown covariance, obtain matching prediction-error bounds across sample size, corruption rate, condition number, and computational budget.
status: A 2026 near-linear-time method uses roughly \(d/\epsilon^4\) samples and achieves \(O(\sqrt{\epsilon\kappa})\) prediction error when \(\epsilon\kappa\lesssim1\); significant tradeoff gaps remain.
why: It would guide robust regression when estimating the covariance accurately is itself expensive.
key_works: Adil, Błasiok, Chen, and Sridharan (2026), *On Efficient Robust Regression with Subquadratic Samples*, PMLR 336:3–74.

title: Robust regression beyond SQ sample barriers
open: Can unrestricted polynomial-time algorithms beat the subquadratic-sample error barriers proved for statistical-query algorithms, or can those barriers be strengthened to broader computational models?
status: The 2026 regression analysis gives an SQ barrier below \(O(\sqrt{\epsilon\kappa})\) and additional low-degree evidence. Neither is a universal polynomial-time impossibility theorem.
why: It distinguishes limitations of current proof models from limitations of robust statistics itself.
key_works: Adil et al. (2026), *On Efficient Robust Regression with Subquadratic Samples*.

title: Optimal Gaussian robust estimation beyond restricted algorithms
open: Determine whether the information-theoretically optimal contamination dependence for high-dimensional Gaussian estimation can be achieved efficiently outside the regimes already ruled out for SQ algorithms.
status: Longstanding statistical–computational gap. SQ lower bounds are substantial evidence but leave the power of more general algorithms unresolved.
why: It would establish whether robust estimation’s logarithmic or polynomial overheads are inherent.
key_works: Diakonikolas, Kane, and Stewart (2017), *Statistical Query Lower Bounds for Robust Estimation of High-dimensional Gaussians and Gaussian Mixtures*, arXiv:1611.03473.

title: Structure-agnostic minimax risk for partially linear models
open: Determine the minimax risk for estimating the linear coefficient when nuisance estimators are available only through black-box error guarantees, and decide whether double machine learning is optimal.
status: Explicit COLT 2025 problem. Structure-aware optimality and selected structure-agnostic results do not settle this general black-box formulation.
why: It tests a major justification for plugging arbitrary machine-learning estimators into causal inference.
key_works: Gu (2025), *Open Problem: Structure-Agnostic Minimax Risk for Partial Linear Model*, PMLR 291:6220–6224.

title: Testable noise assumptions beyond Gaussian halfspaces
open: Characterize concept classes and marginal families for which a polynomial-time learner can both test a noise assumption and certify near-optimal prediction whenever its test accepts.
status: Gaussian-halfspace Massart-noise testing became tractable in 2026. The same work shows that testability can be computationally harder than ordinary learning.
why: It would replace unverifiable modeling assumptions with meaningful acceptance tests.
key_works: Goel, Klivans, Stavropoulos, and Vasilyan (2026), *Testing Noise Assumptions of Learning Algorithms*, PMLR 336:2804–2853.

title: Constant-factor optimality of the Silver rate
open: For predetermined nonnegative GD stepsizes on smooth convex functions, close the subpolynomial gap between the Silver upper bound and the best general lower bound.
status: September 2026 results determine the polynomial exponent \(p=\log_2(1+\sqrt2)\), but the lower bound retains an \(n^{-o(1)}\)-type loss. The exponent itself is no longer the open problem.
why: It would settle whether any asymptotic improvement remains beyond the Silver schedule.
key_works: Altschuler and Parrilo (2025), *Acceleration by Stepsize Hedging I*, arXiv:2309.07879; Ye and Liu (2026), *Silver Rate Is (Almost) Optimal for Gradient Descent Acceleration*, arXiv:2609.09152.

title: Sharp anytime GD rates beyond polynomial exponents
open: Obtain matching constant-factor or sharp logarithmic-factor bounds for infinite predetermined nonnegative schedules that must work at every stopping horizon.
status: Anytime acceleration was established in 2024. The optimal polynomial exponent was identified by 2026 lower bounds; finer asymptotics remain the target.
why: Real training often stops at an unplanned horizon rather than at a schedule’s specially selected endpoint.
key_works: Zhang, Lee, Du, and Chen (2024), *Anytime Acceleration of Gradient Descent*, arXiv:2411.17668; Ye and Liu (2026), *Silver Rate Is (Almost) Optimal*, arXiv:2609.09152.

title: Can signed stepsizes beat nonnegative Silver exponents?
open: Determine the optimal convergence exponent for predetermined GD schedules allowed to contain negative stepsizes, in both fixed-horizon and anytime settings.
status: September 2026 lower bounds beyond the classical first-order barrier allow signed stepsizes, but the sharper Silver-exponent result is stated for nonnegative schedules.
why: It asks whether temporary movement against the gradient fundamentally enlarges stepsize-only optimization power.
key_works: Ye and Liu (2026), *Improved Gradient Descent Lower Bounds Beyond Nesterov*, arXiv:2609.02855; *Silver Rate Is (Almost) Optimal*, arXiv:2609.09152.

title: Exact strongly convex stepsize complexity
open: Close the subpolynomial condition-number gap between strongly convex Silver-schedule upper bounds and universal lower bounds for predetermined nonnegative schedules.
status: September 2026 work matches the polynomial exponent of \(\kappa\), with lower complexity \(\kappa^{1/p-o(1)}\log(1/\delta)\). Exact dependence is the remaining refinement.
why: It would establish the precise price of avoiding momentum in ill-conditioned optimization.
key_works: Liu and Ye (2026), *Silver Rate Is (Almost) Optimal for Gradient Descent: The Strongly Convex Case*, arXiv:2609.26873.

title: Black-box reductions to adaptive nonconvex optimization
open: Construct black-box reductions that transform optimal online convex algorithms into stochastic nonconvex optimizers while preserving meaningful adaptive guarantees.
status: Explicit COLT 2024 problem. The challenge is stronger than obtaining a conventional worst-case stationary-point rate.
why: It could make progress in online learning immediately reusable in practical adaptive optimization.
key_works: Chen and Hazan (2024), *Open Problem: Black-Box Reductions and Adaptive Gradient Methods for Nonconvex Optimization*, PMLR 247.

title: Necessary overparameterization for alternating least squares
open: For rank-\(r\), order-three tensor decomposition from random initialization, can ALS provably succeed with \(k=o(r^2)\) fitted components, or is superlinear overparameterization necessary?
status: Explicit COLT 2026 problem. A cited positive result works with \(k=O(r^2)\); the gap to smaller ranks is unresolved.
why: Reducing unnecessary components would improve tensor learning’s memory, computation, and interpretability.
key_works: Arvanitakis, Srinivas, and Vijayaraghavan (2026), *Open Problem: How Much Overparametrization Is Needed for ALS in Tensor Decomposition?*

title: Sharp stochastic tradeoffs for stepsize-only acceleration
open: Characterize the best simultaneous bias decay and noise amplification achievable by plain SGD with predetermined varying stepsizes and no momentum.
status: Research target. Deterministic stepsize hedging is now well understood at the exponent level; its full finite-sample stochastic frontier is a separate problem.
why: A deterministic speedup is useful for learning only if stochastic gradients do not erase it.
key_works: Altschuler and Parrilo (2025), *Acceleration by Stepsize Hedging I*, arXiv:2309.07879; Chen and Hazan (2024), *Black-Box Reductions and Adaptive Gradient Methods for Nonconvex Optimization*.

title: Finite-precision stability of aggressive schedules
open: Give sharp convergence and error-floor bounds for accelerated stepsize schedules when each gradient and update has bounded or stochastic numerical error.
status: Proposed theory target. Exact-arithmetic acceleration does not itself certify robustness to quantization, rounding, or mixed-precision accumulation.
why: It would determine which provable accelerations survive implementation on low-precision hardware.
key_works: Altschuler and Parrilo (2025), *Acceleration by Stepsize Hedging I*; Zhang et al. (2024), *Anytime Acceleration of Gradient Descent*, arXiv:2411.17668.

title: Practically checkable convergence conditions for Adam
open: Identify conditions on loss geometry, gradient noise, and moment parameters that both explain standard Adam’s successful regimes and can be checked without assuming its convergence.
status: Research target. General convergence is false; modified algorithms and conditional convergence theorems do not provide a complete practical criterion.
why: It would replace optimizer folklore with conditions tied to observable training behavior.
key_works: Reddi, Kale, and Kumar (2018), *On the Convergence of Adam and Beyond*, arXiv:1904.09237.

title: Boundary complexity in discontinuous online optimization
open: Characterize which sequences of piecewise-Lipschitz objectives permit efficient sublinear regret, with sharp dependence on discontinuity geometry rather than only worst-case discretization.
status: Explicit 2026 open-problem program, motivated by data-driven algorithm configuration.
why: Algorithm performance often changes discontinuously with hyperparameters, defeating ordinary smooth optimization theory.
key_works: Balcan, Pegden, and Sharma (2026), *Invited Open Problem: Online Optimization of Piecewise-Lipschitz Functions with Applications to Data-Driven Algorithm Design*.

title: Sharp algorithm-dependent generalization beyond interpolation
open: Derive an efficiently evaluable bound that distinguishes identical architectures trained to interpolate meaningful labels versus random labels, and quantitatively predicts their population-risk difference.
status: Research target motivated by experiments since 2017. Capacity-only explanations and several forms of uniform convergence are insufficient in known constructions.
why: It targets what the training algorithm and data structure contribute beyond parameter count.
key_works: Zhang et al. (2017), *Understanding Deep Learning Requires Rethinking Generalization*, arXiv:1611.03530; Nagarajan and Kolter (2019), *Uniform Convergence May Be Unable to Explain Generalization in Deep Learning*, arXiv:1902.04742.

title: Near-observed-risk PAC-Bayes certificates at modern scale
open: Produce a preregistered generalization certificate within a small specified gap, such as two percentage points, of observed risk for a large trained model without using the evaluation labels to choose the certificate.
status: Proposed quantitative target. Nonvacuous deep-network PAC-Bayes bounds already exist; the open target is sharpness, scale, and clean selection accounting.
why: It would turn theoretical generalization bounds into usable model-release evidence.
key_works: Dziugaite and Roy (2017), *Computing Nonvacuous Generalization Bounds for Deep Stochastic Neural Networks*, arXiv:1703.11008.

title: Reparameterization-invariant complexity with predictive power
open: Construct a tractable complexity measure invariant to function-preserving neural reparameterizations that yields useful risk bounds and distinguishes successful from unsuccessful training.
status: Research target. Existing norm, flatness, and capacity measures capture selected aspects but do not jointly satisfy this specification.
why: A complexity explanation should not change merely because equivalent parameters are rescaled.
key_works: Berner, Grohs, Kutyniok, and Petersen (2021), *The Modern Mathematics of Deep Learning*, arXiv:2105.04026; Nagarajan and Kolter (2019), arXiv:1902.04742.

title: Necessary and sufficient conditions for nonlinear benign overfitting
open: Identify conditions under which an interpolating, feature-learning nonlinear predictor achieves vanishing excess risk despite label noise.
status: Linear-model benign overfitting has precise spectral characterizations. An equally sharp theory covering learned nonlinear features remains a research frontier.
why: It would explain when fitting noise is harmless and when interpolation is dangerous.
key_works: Bartlett, Long, Lugosi, and Tsigler (2020), *Benign Overfitting in Linear Regression*, arXiv:1906.11300; Yang and Hu (2021), *Feature Learning in Infinite-Width Neural Networks*, arXiv:2011.14522.

title: Benign overfitting with dependent training observations
open: Obtain necessary-and-sufficient benign-overfitting criteria for specified dependent designs, such as stationary mixing time series with growing feature dimension.
status: Research target extending independent-design theory. Dependence changes effective information and the interaction between covariance spectra and noise.
why: Most sequential, spatial, and repeated-user datasets are not independent samples.
key_works: Bartlett et al. (2020), *Benign Overfitting in Linear Regression*, arXiv:1906.11300; Holzman et al. (2026), *Uniform Laws of Large Numbers in Product Spaces*, arXiv:2603.24493.

title: Generalization through learned-feature transitions
open: In a specified teacher–student model, derive finite-width risk bounds that remain informative as training transitions from kernel-like behavior to substantial feature learning.
status: Kernel-limit and feature-learning-limit theories both exist. A sharp finite-size bridge between their predictive regimes is not supplied by either limit alone.
why: It would explain when adding width improves a model and when it suppresses useful representation learning.
key_works: Jacot, Gabriel, and Hongler (2018), *Neural Tangent Kernel*, arXiv:1806.07572; Yang and Hu (2021), *Feature Learning in Infinite-Width Neural Networks*, arXiv:2011.14522.

title: Generalization certificates for the entire tuning procedure
open: Certify the risk of the final selected model while accounting for adaptive architecture search, optimizer tuning, checkpoint selection, and repeated validation access.
status: Proposed target. Adaptive-data-analysis theory controls information reuse, but obtaining tight certificates for large realistic tuning pipelines remains a distinct challenge.
why: Certifying a fixed checkpoint after ignoring how it was selected can understate overfitting.
key_works: Dwork et al. (2015), *Generalization in Adaptive Data Analysis and Holdout Reuse*, arXiv:1506.02629; Dziugaite and Roy (2017), arXiv:1703.11008.

title: Quantifying useful versus incidental memorization
open: Define and estimate a decomposition of memorization into information necessary for population performance and information removable without appreciable risk increase.
status: Research target. Interpolation and memorization are empirically established, but fitting examples is not itself a quantitative account of their causal contribution.
why: It would inform compression, privacy, data valuation, and unlearning.
key_works: Zhang et al. (2017), *Understanding Deep Learning Requires Rethinking Generalization*, arXiv:1611.03530; Sekhari et al. (2021), *Remember What You Want to Forget*, arXiv:2103.03279.

title: Which margin solution does deep gradient descent select?
subfield: Neural optimization dynamics and implicit bias
open: Characterize when gradient descent on a homogeneous network converges toward a globally optimal margin solution, versus a particular suboptimal stationary margin configuration.
status: Homogeneous-network results establish important margin-maximization and KKT behavior; they do not generally identify the globally selected solution.
why: Different stationary margin solutions can generalize very differently.
key_works: Soudry et al. (2018), *The Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent on Separable Data*, arXiv:1710.10345; Lyu and Li (2020), *Gradient Descent Maximizes the Margin of Homogeneous Neural Networks*, arXiv:1906.05890.

title: Implicit bias of adaptive stochastic optimizers
subfield: Neural optimization dynamics and implicit bias
open: Determine the predictor selected by Adam-like methods on separable nonlinear models when stochastic noise, moment estimates, and parameter scaling interact.
status: Research target. The implicit bias of ordinary GD in important homogeneous settings is much clearer than that of practical adaptive stochastic training.
why: It would connect optimizer choice directly to the learned function rather than merely convergence speed.
key_works: Soudry et al. (2018), arXiv:1710.10345; Reddi, Kale, and Kumar (2018), *On the Convergence of Adam and Beyond*, arXiv:1904.09237.

title: Finite-width thresholds for feature learning
subfield: Neural optimization dynamics and implicit bias
open: For specified multi-index teacher models, determine the smallest width and training time at which standard randomly initialized SGD learns useful features rather than remaining effectively kernel-like.
status: Research target. Infinite-width feature-learning descriptions and 2026 vanilla-SGD limitations provide partial boundaries, not a complete finite-width phase diagram.
why: It would predict the parameter scale needed for genuine representation learning.
key_works: Yang and Hu (2021), arXiv:2011.14522; Barzilai and Shamir (2026), *Limitations of SGD for Multi-Index Models Beyond Statistical Queries*.

title: Joint depth–width–time limits
subfield: Neural optimization dynamics and implicit bias
open: Derive controlled limits when network depth, width, and training duration grow together, with explicit approximation errors for finite networks.
status: Research target. Taking width to infinity while holding other quantities fixed does not automatically justify simultaneous scaling.
why: Real models become deeper, wider, and longer-trained together.
key_works: Yang and Hu (2021), *Feature Learning in Infinite-Width Neural Networks*, arXiv:2011.14522; Yang et al. (2022), *Tensor Programs V*, arXiv:2203.03466.

title: Predictive theory of the edge of stability
subfield: Neural optimization dynamics and implicit bias
open: Predict the evolving curvature, loss oscillations, and eventual learning progress of finite-step neural GD from measurable properties of the training problem.
status: The edge-of-stability phenomenon was documented in 2021. A broadly predictive, finite-network theory remains a research target.
why: It could explain why practical learning rates operate outside classical monotone-descent conditions.
key_works: Cohen et al. (2021), *Gradient Descent on Neural Networks Typically Occurs at the Edge of Stability*, arXiv:2103.00065.

title: Edge-of-stability dynamics with minibatching and preconditioning
subfield: Neural optimization dynamics and implicit bias
open: Determine which curvature or generalized-stability quantity predicts training behavior when minibatch noise and adaptive preconditioning replace deterministic GD.
status: Research target extending deterministic observations; the Hessian’s largest eigenvalue alone need not capture a history-dependent optimizer.
why: Most large-scale training uses neither full-batch gradients nor an unchanging Euclidean metric.
key_works: Cohen et al. (2021), arXiv:2103.00065; Reddi et al. (2018), arXiv:1904.09237.

title: Complete vanilla-SGD phase diagrams for multi-index models
subfield: Neural optimization dynamics and implicit bias
open: Obtain matching upper and lower bounds for ordinary SGD across signal structure, sample reuse, batch size, learning rate, and network architecture in multi-index learning.
status: A 2026 non-SQ framework gives new lower bounds for standard SGD and identifies shortcomings in older SQ-based predictions.
why: It would identify what standard training actually can learn without algorithmic modifications hidden inside the theorem.
key_works: Barzilai and Shamir (2026), *Limitations of SGD for Multi-Index Models Beyond Statistical Queries*, PMLR 336:559–612.

title: Uniformly reliable hyperparameter transfer
subfield: Neural optimization dynamics and implicit bias
open: Prove finite-width, finite-depth guarantees for transferring learning rates and related hyperparameters from a small model to a substantially larger one.
status: \(\mu\)-parameterization and empirical zero-shot transfer are established. A general guarantee with useful finite-size error and joint depth scaling remains a research target.
why: It could remove much of the expensive hyperparameter search performed at full scale.
key_works: Yang et al. (2022), *Tensor Programs V: Tuning Large Neural Networks via Zero-Shot Hyperparameter Transfer*, arXiv:2203.03466.

title: Exact depth required to compute the maximum with ReLUs
open: Determine the minimum depth required to represent \(\max\{x_1,\ldots,x_d\}\) exactly with unrestricted-width ReLU networks under a clearly specified depth convention.
status: A longstanding depth-separation problem. A 2026 result proves new superlinear width lower bounds at several depths, not the full width-independent depth conjecture.
why: It isolates an elementary function whose exact neural depth complexity remains surprisingly subtle.
key_works: Safran (2026), *A Depth Hierarchy for Computing the Maximum in ReLU Networks via Extremal Graph Theory*, PMLR 336.

title: Fixed-parameter tractability of zonotope norm maximization
open: Can zonotope norm maximization be solved in \(f(d)\operatorname{poly}(n)\) time when input dimension \(d\) is the parameter, or is such an algorithm excluded by parameterized hardness?
status: Explicit COLT 2025 problem. Dimension-dependent enumeration does not establish fixed-parameter tractability.
why: It bears directly on exact Lipschitz constants and verification of shallow ReLU networks.
key_works: Froese, Grillo, Hertrich, and Skutella (2025), *Open Problem: Fixed-Parameter Tractability of Zonotope Problems*.

title: Fixed-parameter tractability of zonotope noncontainment
open: Decide whether zonotope noncontainment admits an FPT algorithm in dimension, or prove an appropriate parameterized lower bound.
status: A separate explicit 2025 problem from norm maximization, with consequences for positivity and comparison of piecewise-linear functions.
why: It would clarify the dimensional barrier in exact neural verification.
key_works: Froese et al. (2025), *Open Problem: Fixed-Parameter Tractability of Zonotope Problems*.

title: Sharp depth–width–precision tradeoffs
open: Characterize the resources needed to approximate a specified smooth compositional function class when depth, width, and weight bit precision are all charged.
status: Research target. Approximation results that count real-valued parameters alone do not determine implementable description complexity.
why: It distinguishes genuine representational efficiency from encoding information in unrealistically precise weights.
key_works: Berner et al. (2021), *The Modern Mathematics of Deep Learning*, arXiv:2105.04026.

title: Efficient discovery of approximate symmetries
open: Learn and exploit approximately valid transformations when the symmetry group is unknown, with guarantees degrading continuously with symmetry violation.
status: Exact invariance for known finite and infinite groups, and selected unknown finite-group settings, received polynomial-time results in 2026. Approximate discovery is a distinct refinement.
why: Real data rarely satisfy the exact symmetries assumed by equivariant models.
key_works: Soleymani, Tahmasebi, Jaillet, and Jegelka (2026), *Efficient Learning and Symmetry Discovery under Exact Invariances*.

title: Verifiable expressivity without exhaustive input enumeration
open: Construct compact certificates that a trained piecewise-linear network implements a specified algorithm or function on an infinite input domain, with independently checkable verification.
status: Proposed infrastructure target. Representation theorems and restricted verification algorithms do not supply a general practical certificate format.
why: It would distinguish “works on tests” from “implements the intended rule.”
key_works: Safran (2026), *A Depth Hierarchy for Computing the Maximum in ReLU Networks*; Froese et al. (2025), *Fixed-Parameter Tractability of Zonotope Problems*.

title: Removing the remaining simultaneous U-calibration overhead
open: Can one forecast sequence achieve \(O(\sqrt T)\) regret for every bounded proper loss while also achieving \(O(\log T)\) for every bounded smooth proper loss, without the extra logarithmic overhead in the general-loss guarantee?
status: In 2026, a single algorithm achieves the smooth-loss logarithmic rate together with a \(\widetilde O(\sqrt T)\) general bound.
why: It asks whether universal forecasts can adapt optimally to all downstream decision-makers at once.
key_works: Frongillo, Luo, Mehta, and Schneider (2026), *Toward Simultaneously Optimal Regret in U-Calibration*.

title: U-calibration for genuinely multidimensional outcomes
open: Establish sharp simultaneously adaptive regret guarantees for a useful family of proper losses on multiclass or vector-valued outcomes.
status: Research target extending binary forecasting results. The geometry and boundary behavior of multidimensional probability predictions create additional obstacles.
why: Most deployed forecasting systems predict more than a single binary event.
key_works: Frongillo et al. (2026), *Toward Simultaneously Optimal Regret in U-Calibration*; Gibbs and Tibshirani (2026), *Sample-Efficient Omniprediction for Proper Losses*.

title: Efficient sequential omniprediction under distribution change
open: Maintain one predictor competitive for many downstream proper losses when contexts and outcome distributions change, with regret adapting to a specified variation budget.
status: Research target. Sample-efficient static omniprediction does not automatically provide sequential adaptation under drift.
why: A shared forecast should remain useful to different consumers as conditions evolve.
key_works: Gibbs and Tibshirani (2026), *Sample-Efficient Omniprediction for Proper Losses*; Gibbs and Candès (2021), *Adaptive Conformal Inference Under Distribution Shift*, arXiv:2106.00170.

title: Minimal sufficient calibration for a downstream task family
open: Given a family of decision losses, characterize the weakest calibration or moment conditions sufficient for near-optimal downstream decisions, with matching sample complexity.
status: Research target sharpened by 2026 lower bounds showing multicalibration can be strictly harder than omniprediction.
why: It could avoid paying for stronger statistical guarantees than the application needs.
key_works: Gibbs and Tibshirani (2026), *Sample-Efficient Omniprediction for Proper Losses*; Hébert-Johnson et al. (2018), *Calibration for the Computationally-Identifiable Masses*, arXiv:1711.08513.

title: Sharp learnability of nonstationary partial-monitoring games
open: Characterize achievable regret when feedback is indirect and the loss-generating environment changes under explicit variation constraints.
status: Research target. General interactive complexity frameworks cover important stationary or adversarial formulations but do not collapse all nonstationary feedback structures into one sharp criterion.
why: Many systems observe proxies, delayed signals, or only consequences of their own actions.
key_works: Foster, Foster, Golowich, and Rakhlin (2023), *On the Complexity of Multi-Agent Decision Making: From Learning in Games to Partial Monitoring*, arXiv:2305.00684.

title: Learning changing strategic-response models
open: Obtain regret guarantees when agents’ manipulation costs or feasible responses are unknown and change, while distinguishing learning the environment from influencing it.
status: Research target. It is not the older fixed-model strategic-classification regret question; the unresolved specification includes unknown, evolving response structure.
why: Predictors deployed in markets, admissions, or ranking systems change the behavior they observe.
key_works: Perdomo et al. (2020), *Performative Prediction*, arXiv:2002.06673; Foster et al. (2023), *On the Complexity of Multi-Agent Decision Making*, arXiv:2305.00684.

title: Sharp dimensional dependence in bandit convex optimization
open: Determine matching minimax regret dependence on dimension and horizon for specified stochastic or adversarial bandit-convex-optimization models.
status: Longstanding; recent Thompson-sampling and lower-bound work continue to refine the dimensional frontier. Model assumptions must be fixed before comparing rates.
why: It would quantify the intrinsic price of optimizing a high-dimensional function from scalar feedback.
key_works: Bakhtiari, Lattimore, and Szepesvári (2025), *Thompson Sampling for Bandit Convex Optimisation*, PMLR 291.

title: Heavy-tailed bandits with unknown moment parameters
open: Determine the optimal cost of adapting to unknown finite-moment order and moment bound, or identify the weakest additional assumptions permitting near-oracle regret.
status: Explicit COLT 2025 problem. Most guarantees assume these parameters are known; unrestricted adaptation cannot simply be presumed free.
why: Real reward distributions rarely arrive with certified tail parameters.
key_works: Genalti and Metelli (2025), *Open Problem: Regret Minimization in Heavy-Tailed Bandits with Unknown Distributional Parameters*.

title: Joint differential privacy in linear contextual bandits
open: Determine the sharp privacy cost in linear contextual-bandit regret, including dimension, horizon, privacy parameters, and the distinction between public and private contexts.
status: Explicit COLT 2024 problem; precise model distinctions are central to the unresolved complexity comparison.
why: It measures whether sequential personalization can preserve each user’s privacy without prohibitive learning loss.
key_works: Azize and Basu (2024), *Open Problem: What Is the Complexity of Joint Differential Privacy in Linear Contextual Bandits?*

title: Tight discrete-time adaptive RKHS confidence bounds
open: Obtain sharp confidence radii for kernel regression with adaptively chosen covariates, specifying when information-gain or dimension factors can be reduced.
status: Posed in 2021. A 2023 lower bound rules out certain improvements in a continuous-time formulation; remaining discrete-time and structured-kernel refinements must respect that barrier.
why: Confidence width directly determines exploration efficiency in kernel bandits and control.
key_works: Vakili, Scarlett, and Javidi (2021), *Open Problem: Tight Online Confidence Intervals for RKHS Elements*; Lattimore (2023), *A Lower Bound for Linear and Kernel Regression with Adaptive Covariates*.

title: Instance-optimal equilibrium identification in matrix games
open: Characterize the instance-dependent samples needed to identify a Nash equilibrium of a noisy two-player zero-sum matrix game, with matching algorithms and lower bounds.
status: Explicit COLT 2025 problem. Worst-case rates do not capture the full payoff-gap and equilibrium-geometry dependence.
why: It generalizes best-arm identification to competitive decisions with mixed strategies.
key_works: Maiti (2025), *Open Problem: Optimal Instance-Dependent Sample Complexity for Finding Nash Equilibrium in Two Player Zero-Sum Matrix Games*.

title: Computable instance-optimal exploration allocations
open: Turn information-theoretic optimal exploration allocations into polynomial-time algorithms for structured bandit classes where the allocation problem itself is difficult.
status: Research target. Statistical characterizations can conceal an optimization problem as hard as the original decision problem.
why: It would make instance-optimal sample efficiency operational rather than purely existential.
key_works: Foster et al. (2021), *The Statistical Complexity of Interactive Decision Making*, arXiv:2112.13487; Chen et al. (2024), *Assouad, Fano, and Le Cam with Interaction*, arXiv:2410.05117.

title: Order-optimal regret for kernel reinforcement learning
open: Obtain matching regret bounds for kernel-based RL with explicit horizon, kernel-complexity, and accuracy dependence.
status: Explicit COLT 2024 problem. Reward-free sample-complexity results do not automatically resolve online regret.
why: It would make nonlinear function approximation’s exploration cost quantitatively predictable.
key_works: Vakili (2024), *Open Problem: Order Optimal Regret Bounds for Kernel-Based Reinforcement Learning*; Domingues et al. (2020), *Kernel-Based Reinforcement Learning: A Finite-Time Analysis*, arXiv:2004.05599.

title: Computationally efficient DEC-optimal reinforcement learning
open: Identify broad model classes for which decision-estimation-coefficient guarantees can be attained with polynomial-time computation and implementable estimation oracles.
status: Research target. DEC gives powerful statistical characterizations, but statistical complexity and computational tractability remain distinct.
why: It could unify provably efficient RL without hiding expensive planning or model-selection subroutines.
key_works: Foster et al. (2021), *The Statistical Complexity of Interactive Decision Making*, arXiv:2112.13487.

title: Sharp rather than polynomial-factor interactive complexity
open: Close remaining polynomial-factor gaps between general interactive lower-bound characterizations and achievable regret or sample complexity for specified convex model classes.
status: A 2024 framework unifies interactive Assouad, Fano, and Le Cam arguments and gives broad learnability characterizations; sharp rates remain a finer target.
why: Polynomial losses can determine whether a theoretically learnable system is usable.
key_works: Chen, Foster, Han, Qian, Rakhlin, and Xu (2024), *Assouad, Fano, and Le Cam with Interaction*, arXiv:2410.05117.

title: Offline policy evaluation with unknown behavior policy
open: Under trajectory data, linear realizability of policy values, and concentrability, determine when statistically efficient policy evaluation remains possible without knowing the behavior policy.
status: A 2026 positive theorem assumes the behavior policy is known. Removing that information is a distinct question, not the already resolved known-policy case.
why: Logged datasets often omit exact action propensities or were produced by changing systems.
key_works: Tkachuk, Szepesvári, and Tan (2026), *Trajectory Data Suffices for Statistically Efficient Policy Evaluation in Fixed-Horizon Offline RL with Linear \(q^\pi\)-Realizability and Concentrability*.

title: Computational tractability of trajectory-based offline RL
open: Determine whether the strongest statistically efficient trajectory-based offline-RL guarantees admit polynomial-time implementations under explicit function-class access.
status: Research target. Trajectories can overcome certain statistical impossibilities for unstructured transition samples, but that does not by itself settle computational efficiency.
why: It separates the value of richer logs from the cost of processing them.
key_works: Tkachuk et al. (2026), *Trajectory Data Suffices…*; Levine et al. (2020), *Offline Reinforcement Learning: Tutorial, Review, and Perspectives on Open Problems*, arXiv:2005.01643.

title: Model-free DEC guarantees with realistic function approximation
open: Attain model-free DEC-style exploration guarantees using practical regression or representation-learning primitives rather than inaccessible optimization over abstract function classes.
status: Research target following the 2022 model-free DEC framework.
why: It would connect unifying RL theory to actual value-based training systems.
key_works: Foster, Golowich, Qian, Rakhlin, and Sekhari (2022), *Model-Free Reinforcement Learning with the Decision-Estimation Coefficient*, arXiv:2211.14250.

title: Minimal exploratory identifiability for partially observed systems
open: Characterize the weakest quantitative observability conditions under which an agent can both identify a partially observed environment and learn a near-optimal policy efficiently.
status: Research target. Identifiability from ideal experiments is weaker than identifiability through actions an initially ignorant agent can afford to take.
why: It addresses learning when observations do not reveal the true state.
key_works: Foster et al. (2021), *The Statistical Complexity of Interactive Decision Making*, arXiv:2112.13487; Levine et al. (2020), arXiv:2005.01643.

title: Learning safe exploratory policies without a perfect safety model
open: Under explicit recoverability and safe-initial-policy assumptions, derive matching sample and regret bounds for learning while limiting the probability of constraint violation.
status: Research target; unrestricted safe exploration is impossible without structural assumptions or prior safe access.
why: It would quantify the information price of avoiding catastrophic experiments.
key_works: Foster et al. (2021), *The Statistical Complexity of Interactive Decision Making*, arXiv:2112.13487; Levine et al. (2020), *Offline Reinforcement Learning*, arXiv:2005.01643.

title: Sharp horizon dependence in imitation under distribution shift
open: Characterize the exact horizon penalty for behavior cloning when errors, dynamics stability, and expert coverage are jointly specified rather than bounded independently.
status: Recent work substantially revises simple compounding-error folklore. A complete instance-sensitive horizon theory remains a research target.
why: It would explain when supervised imitation suffices and when interaction is necessary.
key_works: Foster, Block, and Misra (2024), *Is Behavior Cloning All You Need? Understanding Horizon in Imitation Learning*, arXiv:2407.15007.

title: Reliable policy selection with learned, exploitable evaluators
open: Bound actual task performance when policy search adaptively exploits an imperfect learned evaluator, including correlated errors across candidate trajectories.
status: Research target. Results for fixed candidate distributions or pairwise win-rate do not cover unrestricted adaptive policy improvement.
why: It addresses reward hacking as a statistical interaction problem rather than merely an anecdotal failure.
key_works: Sriraman and Block (2026), *Revisiting the Suboptimality of Best-of-N for Inference-Time Alignment*; Foster et al. (2023), *On the Complexity of Multi-Agent Decision Making*, arXiv:2305.00684.

title: Learning augmentations rather than assuming them
subfield: Representation learning, active learning, and continual learning
open: Learn an augmentation mechanism from unlabeled data that provably preserves downstream-relevant information and yields a sample-efficiency gain under explicit structural assumptions.
status: Research target. Contrastive theories often assume useful positive-pair structure instead of deriving it from the available observations.
why: An incorrect augmentation can erase the very signal that the downstream task needs.
key_works: Arora et al. (2019), *A Theoretical Analysis of Contrastive Unsupervised Representation Learning*, arXiv:1902.09229; HaoChen et al. (2021), *Provable Guarantees for Self-Supervised Deep Learning with Spectral Contrastive Loss*, arXiv:2106.04156.

title: Optimal negative sampling for downstream risk
subfield: Representation learning, active learning, and continual learning
open: Determine the negative-sampling distribution and number of negatives minimizing downstream excess risk when false negatives and class imbalance are explicitly modeled.
status: Research target. Latent-class contrastive theory supplies useful baselines but not a universal downstream-optimal sampling rule.
why: It could prevent expensive contrastive training from optimizing the wrong discrimination problem.
key_works: Arora et al. (2019), *A Theoretical Analysis of Contrastive Unsupervised Representation Learning*, arXiv:1902.09229.

title: Nonasymptotic pretraining–finetuning interaction
subfield: Representation learning, active learning, and continual learning
open: Derive sharp finite-sample downstream-risk bounds jointly in unlabeled pretraining size, labeled finetuning size, representation dimension, and symmetry-related nonidentifiability.
status: A 2026 two-stage M-estimation theory characterizes limiting risk distributions for important examples; finite-sample sharpness is the remaining target.
why: It would tell practitioners how to allocate data between pretraining and task-specific supervision.
key_works: Tinati and Tu (2026), *On the Asymptotics of Self-Supervised Pre-training: Two-Stage M-Estimation and Representation Symmetry*.

title: Representation transfer with changing task families
subfield: Representation learning, active learning, and continual learning
open: Characterize when a representation learned for one distribution of tasks remains sample-efficient for a different task distribution, with a measurable transfer-distance term.
status: Research target. Downstream guarantees are commonly conditional on compatibility between pretraining structure and target tasks.
why: It would distinguish reusable representations from benchmark-specific shortcuts.
key_works: Arora et al. (2019), arXiv:1902.09229; Tinati and Tu (2026), *On the Asymptotics of Self-Supervised Pre-training*.

title: Minimal auxiliary information for nonlinear disentanglement
subfield: Representation learning, active learning, and continual learning
open: Determine the minimum amount and form of auxiliary information needed to identify nonlinear latent factors, with matching lower bounds.
status: Unrestricted unsupervised disentanglement is already nonidentifiable. Auxiliary-variable nonlinear-ICA results establish positive regimes but not a universal minimal-information frontier.
why: It would specify what extra labels, environments, temporal structure, or interventions are actually necessary.
key_works: Locatello et al. (2019), *Challenging Common Assumptions in the Unsupervised Learning of Disentangled Representations*, arXiv:1811.12359; Khemakhem et al. (2020), *Variational Autoencoders and Nonlinear ICA*, arXiv:1907.04809.

title: Active learning with only physically realizable queries
subfield: Representation learning, active learning, and continual learning
open: Determine sharp label complexity and efficient algorithms when queries must be selected from naturally occurring or physically realizable inputs, not arbitrary synthesized points.
status: Research target. The distinction is important even for halfspaces; 2026 work explicitly studies active learning without synthetic data.
why: Many theoretical queries cannot be posed to a human, laboratory, or deployed system.
key_works: Black, Larsen, Mazumdar, Saha, and So (2026), *Actively Learning Halfspaces without Synthetic Data*, COLT 2026.

title: Adaptation to unknown active-learning noise structure
subfield: Representation learning, active learning, and continual learning
open: Design computationally efficient active learners that adapt to an unknown noise or disagreement regime without losing the optimal label-complexity advantage.
status: Research target. Different favorable-noise assumptions yield different gains; testing those assumptions can itself be difficult.
why: It would make label-saving algorithms robust to uncertainty about their own prerequisites.
key_works: Goel et al. (2026), *Testing Noise Assumptions of Learning Algorithms*; Black et al. (2026), *Actively Learning Halfspaces without Synthetic Data*.

title: Detecting when unlabeled data will cause negative transfer
subfield: Representation learning, active learning, and continual learning
open: Under a specified cluster or multiview model family, construct a test deciding whether additional unlabeled data can improve supervised risk, with controlled false assurances.
status: Proposed target. Unlabeled data cannot guarantee improvement without assumptions; the challenge is to make useful assumptions partially testable.
why: It would prevent pretraining or semisupervised learning from silently degrading a task.
key_works: Locatello et al. (2019), arXiv:1811.12359; Arora et al. (2019), arXiv:1902.09229.

title: Memory–forgetting–transfer tradeoffs in continual learning
subfield: Representation learning, active learning, and continual learning
open: Determine minimax retained risk and forward-transfer gains as functions of memory, task similarity, number of tasks, and revisitation frequency.
status: Research target. Existing positive results depend strongly on task structure; a general resource-sensitive characterization is absent from the cited framework.
why: It would quantify how much persistent information a continually learning system must retain.
key_works: Schliserman, Buzaglo, Evron, and Soudry (2026), *Convergence of Continual Learning in Homogeneous Deep Networks*.

title: Global recoverability in nonlinear continual learning
subfield: Representation learning, active learning, and continual learning
open: Identify checkable structural conditions guaranteeing global convergence under sequential task training, beyond local regularity conditions.
status: A 2026 analysis proves that global convergence can fail even in simple nonlinear parameterizations, while establishing local linear convergence under regularity assumptions.
why: It distinguishes recoverable forgetting from irreversible movement into bad task-interaction states.
key_works: Schliserman et al. (2026), *Convergence of Continual Learning in Homogeneous Deep Networks*.

title: When SGD learns an in-context algorithm
open: For a specified distribution of regression or classification tasks, prove that ordinary transformer training learns an in-context algorithm with near-optimal finite-sample risk.
status: Transformers can represent useful statistical procedures, and experiments demonstrate learning in-context behavior. Representation and training success are not the same theorem.
why: It would explain why pretraining produces learning algorithms rather than only flexible predictors.
key_works: Garg et al. (2022), *What Can Transformers Learn In-Context?*, arXiv:2208.01066; Bai et al. (2023), *Transformers as Statisticians*, arXiv:2306.04637.

title: In-context adaptation to unseen task priors
open: Quantify the risk of an in-context learner when the deployment task prior differs from the pretraining prior, and determine what adaptation is possible from the prompt alone.
status: Research target. Existing task-family analyses often assume a specified training distribution.
why: Real users present task families not sampled from a model’s pretraining experiment.
key_works: Bai et al. (2023), *Transformers as Statisticians*, arXiv:2306.04637; Akyürek et al. (2023), *What Learning Algorithm Is In-Context Learning?*, arXiv:2211.15661.

title: Robust in-context estimation with corrupted demonstrations
open: Characterize achievable risk when a bounded fraction of prompt demonstrations are adversarially mislabeled, duplicated, or selected, and prove whether standard training discovers robust estimators.
status: Research target extending clean synthetic-task analyses.
why: Demonstrations in real prompts are neither guaranteed independent nor guaranteed correct.
key_works: Garg et al. (2022), arXiv:2208.01066; Akyürek et al. (2023), arXiv:2211.15661.

title: Finite-precision length generalization
open: Prove that a trained transformer implements a specified sequence algorithm beyond training lengths while accounting for bounded precision, accumulated numerical error, and positional encoding.
status: Research target. Expressivity or finite-context learning guarantees do not imply unbounded length extrapolation.
why: It separates genuine algorithm learning from interpolation over familiar sequence lengths.
key_works: Yang, Srebro, and Li (2026), *Tight Sample Complexity of Transformers*; Giapitzakis et al. (2026), *On the Statistical Query Complexity of Learning Semiautomata*.

title: Computational learning complexity of bounded transformers
open: Determine efficient learnability or hardness for transformers with explicitly bounded depth, heads, weight precision, and context length under a specified data distribution.
status: Nearly tight VC/sample-complexity results appeared in 2026; these do not settle the computational cost of finding a good predictor.
why: It distinguishes statistically adequate datasets from algorithmically learnable architectures.
key_works: Yang, Srebro, and Li (2026), *Tight Sample Complexity of Transformers*, PMLR 336.

title: Learning semiautomata beyond statistical queries
open: Determine whether efficient non-SQ algorithms can learn the semiautomata families underlying recent SQ hardness results, or establish broader computational hardness.
status: A 2026 result proves SQ hardness under uniform words and initial states using transition structure rather than only parity-like output languages.
why: It tests the limits of learning latent state-transition algorithms from sequences.
key_works: Giapitzakis, Fountoulakis, Nichani, and Lee (2026), *On the Statistical Query Complexity of Learning Semiautomata: A Random Walk Approach*.

title: Compositional error control for learned reasoning procedures
open: Give end-to-end error guarantees when learned subprocedures are composed adaptively, allowing correlated mistakes rather than assuming independent per-step errors.
status: Research target. Guarantees for isolated in-context estimators do not automatically survive adaptive multi-step composition.
why: A small local error can become a large failure probability in long reasoning chains.
key_works: Bai et al. (2023), *Transformers as Statisticians*, arXiv:2306.04637; Foster, Block, and Misra (2024), *Is Behavior Cloning All You Need?*, arXiv:2407.15007.

title: Task-aware lower bounds for context compression
open: Determine the minimum memory needed to preserve a transformer’s answers for a specified query distribution, rather than preserving all token representations uniformly.
status: Proposed target. General architecture sample complexity does not characterize the information that a particular downstream task must retain.
why: It would give principled limits and objectives for context and cache compression.
key_works: Yang, Srebro, and Li (2026), *Tight Sample Complexity of Transformers*; Bai et al. (2023), arXiv:2306.04637.

title: Deriving language-model scaling exponents
subfield: Scaling laws, grokking, and mechanistic explanations
open: Derive predictive loss-scaling exponents from explicit assumptions about data structure, architecture, and optimization rather than fitting them after training.
status: Empirical power laws have been documented since 2020. A broadly predictive first-principles account remains a research target.
why: It would make scaling forecasts falsifiable outside the range used to fit them.
key_works: Kaplan et al. (2020), *Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models*, arXiv:2001.08361; Hoffmann et al. (2022), *Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models*, arXiv:2203.15556.

title: Joint training-and-inference compute optimality
subfield: Scaling laws, grokking, and mechanistic explanations
open: Optimize model size, data volume, training duration, and inference-time computation for a specified lifetime query distribution and quality constraint.
status: Training-compute allocation has strong empirical baselines. Joint lifetime optimization is a different target because inference demand changes the objective.
why: The cheapest model to train need not be the cheapest system to operate.
key_works: Hoffmann et al. (2022), *Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models*, arXiv:2203.15556; Sriraman and Block (2026), *Revisiting the Suboptimality of Best-of-N*.

title: Scaling with redundant and adaptively reused data
subfield: Scaling laws, grokking, and mechanistic explanations
open: Predict learning curves when examples are correlated, duplicated, repeatedly replayed, or selected adaptively, using a measurable notion of information rather than raw token count.
status: Research target. Conventional fitted scaling variables do not uniquely measure novel statistical information.
why: It would improve decisions about data collection versus additional epochs.
key_works: Kaplan et al. (2020), arXiv:2001.08361; Hoffmann et al. (2022), arXiv:2203.15556; Holzman et al. (2026), arXiv:2603.24493.

title: Predicting grokking time before generalization occurs
subfield: Scaling laws, grokking, and mechanistic explanations
open: Predict the onset time and probability of delayed generalization from early training measurements across a specified family of algorithmic tasks.
status: Grokking was documented in 2022, and mechanistic progress measures exist for selected tasks. A transferable quantitative predictor remains a target.
why: It would distinguish productive long training from futile memorization.
key_works: Power et al. (2022), *Grokking*, arXiv:2201.02177; Nanda et al. (2023), *Progress Measures for Grokking via Mechanistic Interpretability*, arXiv:2301.05217.

title: Genuine emergence versus measurement artifacts
subfield: Scaling laws, grokking, and mechanistic explanations
open: Design preregistered experiments that distinguish discontinuities in underlying capability from discontinuities introduced by thresholded metrics, finite test sets, or task aggregation.
status: Metric-induced apparent emergence was demonstrated in 2023. Whether a particular claimed transition is genuinely structural requires a separate measurement design.
why: It would make claims about sudden capability growth scientifically discriminating.
key_works: Schaeffer, Miranda, and Koyejo (2023), *Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage?*, arXiv:2304.15004; Srivastava et al. (2022), *Beyond the Imitation Game*, arXiv:2206.04615.

title: Identifiability of superposed features
subfield: Scaling laws, grokking, and mechanistic explanations
open: Under an explicit generative model, determine when a learned representation’s constituent features are uniquely recoverable, up to stated symmetries, from activations and interventions.
status: Toy superposition models expose useful mechanisms, but recovering a unique feature ontology from arbitrary activations is not guaranteed.
why: It would clarify whether interpretability methods discover real structure or one of many equivalent decompositions.
key_works: Elhage et al. (2022), *Toy Models of Superposition*, arXiv:2209.10652; Locatello et al. (2019), arXiv:1811.12359.

title: Causally selective feature editing
subfield: Scaling laws, grokking, and mechanistic explanations
open: Modify an identified internal feature while provably preserving a specified set of unrelated model behaviors over a defined input distribution.
status: Proposed target. Finding a correlated feature or a successful local intervention does not establish selective causal control.
why: It would turn interpretability into controlled model repair.
key_works: Elhage et al. (2022), *Toy Models of Superposition*, arXiv:2209.10652; Nanda et al. (2023), arXiv:2301.05217.

title: Completeness certificates for mechanistic explanations
subfield: Scaling laws, grokking, and mechanistic explanations
open: Certify that an extracted circuit explains a specified fraction of a model’s behavior, including counterfactual interventions and out-of-sample inputs.
status: Proposed target. Demonstrating that a circuit is influential is weaker than showing that omitted mechanisms are negligible.
why: It would prevent partial explanations from being mistaken for complete accounts.
key_works: Nanda et al. (2023), *Progress Measures for Grokking via Mechanistic Interpretability*, arXiv:2301.05217; Ribeiro, Singh, and Guestrin (2016), *Why Should I Trust You?*, arXiv:1602.04938.

title: End-to-end computational complexity of score learning and sampling
subfield: Diffusion, flow matching, and generative learning
open: Obtain matching total data, training-computation, and sampling-computation bounds for a concrete distribution family, rather than assuming access to accurate scores.
status: Accurate-score sampling guarantees are established, and 2026 work connects scores to density and parameter estimation. End-to-end computational optimality remains family-dependent.
why: A fast sampler is not a fast generative learner when learning its score is the dominant cost.
key_works: Song et al. (2021), *Score-Based Generative Modeling through Stochastic Differential Equations*, arXiv:2011.13456; Chewi et al. (2026), *DDPM Score Matching and Distribution Learning*.

title: Adaptive diffusion learning on unknown manifolds
subfield: Diffusion, flow matching, and generative learning
open: Achieve sharp end-to-end rates adapting to unknown intrinsic dimension, curvature, and noise thickness without paying unnecessary ambient-dimensional costs.
status: Low-dimensional diffusion theory has advanced through 2026. The target combines adaptation, geometric uncertainty, and computational guarantees rather than asking whether intrinsic-dimension results exist at all.
why: High-dimensional observations often lie near much smaller latent spaces.
key_works: Chakraborty, Berthet, and Bartlett (2026), *Generalization Properties of Score-Matching Diffusion Models for Intrinsically Low-Dimensional Data*, arXiv:2603.03700; Song et al. (2021), arXiv:2011.13456.

title: Tractable subclasses of Gaussian-mixture score learning
subfield: Diffusion, flow matching, and generative learning
open: Characterize structural conditions on Gaussian mixtures under which score estimation is polynomial-time feasible at statistically efficient accuracy.
status: Positive mixture-learning results coexist with 2026 computational and cryptographic lower bounds for general score-estimation families.
why: It would distinguish realistic tractable mixture structure from impossible general-purpose promises.
key_works: Chen, Kontonis, and Shah (2025), *Learning General Gaussian Mixtures with Efficient Score Matching*; Chewi et al. (2026), *DDPM Score Matching and Distribution Learning*.

title: Certified few-step generative sampling
subfield: Diffusion, flow matching, and generative learning
open: Identify broad distribution classes admitting one-to-ten-step sampling with a rigorous distributional-error guarantee and account for the computation needed to learn the accelerated sampler.
