status: Proposed quantitative target. Fast empirical generation does not itself establish distributional accuracy or end-to-end computational savings.
why: It could reduce generative inference latency and energy by an order of magnitude without hiding quality loss.
key_works: Ho, Jain, and Abbeel (2020), *Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models*, arXiv:2006.11239; Lipman et al. (2023), *Flow Matching for Generative Modeling*, arXiv:2210.02747.

title: Robust conditional guidance under score misspecification
subfield: Diffusion, flow matching, and generative learning
open: Quantify how conditional guidance amplifies score-estimation error, and design guidance rules with certified tradeoffs between constraint satisfaction and distributional fidelity.
status: Research target. Guarantees for an unconditional learned sampler do not automatically survive aggressive conditioning.
why: Many useful generation tasks require conditioning on rare or difficult constraints.
key_works: Song et al. (2021), arXiv:2011.13456; Moitra, Risteski, and Rohatgi (2026), *Steering Diffusion Models with Quadratic Rewards: A Fine-Grained Analysis*.

title: Masked-diffusion scheduling with learnable structural knowledge
subfield: Diffusion, flow matching, and generative learning
open: Identify structural information about a target distribution that can be learned efficiently and is sufficient to choose a near-optimal parallel unmasking schedule.
status: A 2026 characterization gives optimal schedules in principle, but also proves that competing with them without strong prior information can be impossible.
why: It targets the actual information needed to turn parallel token generation into a reliable speedup.
key_works: Chen, Cong, and Li (2026), *Optimal Inference Schedules for Masked Diffusion Models*.

title: Instance-optimal discrete diffusion beyond a fixed sampler family
subfield: Diffusion, flow matching, and generative learning
open: Determine the optimal sampling cost for structured discrete distributions over all admissible samplers, and compare it with information-adaptive \(\tau\)-leaping guarantees.
status: In 2026, sharp bounds and algorithmic lower bounds were established for important discrete-diffusion samplers; they are not automatically universal lower bounds over every sampler.
why: It separates limitations of a discretization method from intrinsic generative complexity.
key_works: Dmitriev, Huang, and Wei (2026), *Efficient Sampling with Discrete Diffusion Models: Sharp and Adaptive Guarantees*.

title: Optimal flow-matching couplings under a model-complexity budget
subfield: Diffusion, flow matching, and generative learning
open: Choose training couplings and probability paths minimizing the combined approximation, optimization, and numerical-integration cost of a finite-capacity flow model.
status: Research target. A mathematically valid transport path need not be the easiest path for a given network to learn or integrate.
why: It would connect transport geometry directly to end-to-end generative efficiency.
key_works: Lipman et al. (2023), *Flow Matching for Generative Modeling*, arXiv:2210.02747.

title: Minimal interventions for latent causal identification
open: Determine the minimum number and type of interventions needed to identify a latent causal graph and its variables under an explicit nonlinear observation model.
status: Research target. Causal representation learning supplies positive identifiable regimes, but minimal intervention complexity depends strongly on the observation and intervention classes.
why: It would guide the design of experiments that reveal causal variables rather than merely predictive features.
key_works: Schölkopf et al. (2021), *Towards Causal Representation Learning*, arXiv:2102.11107; Khemakhem et al. (2020), arXiv:1907.04809.

title: Unknown-target soft interventions
open: Identify causal structure when environments apply unknown soft interventions to unknown subsets of latent mechanisms, with finite-sample guarantees.
status: Research target. Knowing which mechanism changed is a stronger assumption than observing only that environments differ.
why: Natural experiments and observational environments rarely provide intervention labels.
key_works: Schölkopf et al. (2021), *Towards Causal Representation Learning*, arXiv:2102.11107; Peters, Bühlmann, and Meinshausen (2016), *Causal Inference Using Invariant Prediction*, arXiv:1501.01332.

title: Stable nonlinear-ICA identifiability
open: Convert qualitative nonlinear-ICA identifiability into sharp finite-sample recovery bounds when auxiliary variation is weak and assumptions are approximately satisfied.
status: Research target. Identifiability in the infinite-data, correctly specified setting does not ensure numerically stable recovery.
why: It would reveal whether theoretically identifiable latent variables can actually be estimated from available data.
key_works: Khemakhem, Kingma, Monti, and Hyvärinen (2020), *Variational Autoencoders and Nonlinear ICA: A Unifying Framework*, arXiv:1907.04809.

title: Transporting causal predictions with hidden confounding
open: Characterize which target-environment causal or interventional predictions are identifiable from multiple source environments when some confounders remain unobserved.
status: Research target. Invariance alone does not resolve every transport problem, especially when the hidden mechanisms differ.
why: It would determine when causal models genuinely support deployment beyond their training environment.
key_works: Peters et al. (2016), *Causal Inference Using Invariant Prediction*, arXiv:1501.01332; Schölkopf et al. (2021), arXiv:2102.11107.

title: Learning cyclic causal mechanisms from limited interventions
open: Under explicit stability and functional assumptions, identify feedback mechanisms and intervention effects in nonlinear cyclic systems from limited perturbations.
status: Research target. Acyclic structural assumptions and equilibrium observations do not automatically identify dynamic feedback.
why: Biological, economic, and controlled systems often contain feedback loops.
key_works: Schölkopf et al. (2021), *Towards Causal Representation Learning*, arXiv:2102.11107; Perdomo et al. (2020), *Performative Prediction*, arXiv:2002.06673.

title: Useful partial identification of learned counterfactuals
open: Produce computationally tractable, sharp counterfactual bounds when observational and intervention data identify only an equivalence class of latent causal models.
status: Research target. Selecting one plausible generative model is not a certificate that its counterfactuals are uniquely determined.
why: It would replace unjustified point counterfactuals with honest, decision-relevant uncertainty.
key_works: Schölkopf et al. (2021), arXiv:2102.11107; Locatello et al. (2019), arXiv:1811.12359.

title: Cost-optimal adaptive causal experimentation
open: Learn an intervention policy minimizing total experimental cost needed to identify a specified causal effect, allowing heterogeneous costs and latent uncertainty.
status: Research target at the intersection of causal identification and interactive decision complexity.
why: The most informative experiment may be expensive, unsafe, or impossible to repeat.
key_works: Peters et al. (2016), arXiv:1501.01332; Foster et al. (2021), *The Statistical Complexity of Interactive Decision Making*, arXiv:2112.13487.

title: Distinguishing causal invariance from accidental stability
open: Design tests that distinguish genuinely mechanism-preserving predictors from predictors that happen to remain accurate across the observed environments.
status: Proposed target. Finite observed environments may fail to expose spurious invariances.
why: It would make claims of causal generalization falsifiable.
key_works: Peters et al. (2016), *Causal Inference Using Invariant Prediction*, arXiv:1501.01332; Arjovsky et al. (2019), *Invariant Risk Minimization*, arXiv:1907.02893.

title: Sharp robustness–accuracy frontiers for realistic generative models
subfield: Robustness, domain shift, and performative effects
open: Determine the achievable clean-risk versus adversarial-risk frontier for a specified nonlinear data-generating model, including computational restrictions.
status: Existence of robustness–accuracy tension is established. The frontier is model-dependent, not a universal fixed penalty.
why: It would distinguish unavoidable tradeoffs from shortcomings of current training methods.
key_works: Tsipras et al. (2019), *Robustness May Be at Odds with Accuracy*, arXiv:1805.12152; Bubeck, Price, and Razenshteyn (2018), *Adversarial Examples from Computational Constraints*, arXiv:1805.10204.

title: Robust sample complexity with learned geometric structure
subfield: Robustness, domain shift, and performative effects
open: Determine when learning a data manifold or invariance structure reduces the additional samples needed for adversarial robustness.
status: Robust generalization can require more data even in simple models. Whether structure-learning removes particular gaps is a separate, model-specific question.
why: It would identify when unlabeled or geometric information can substitute for costly robust labels.
key_works: Schmidt et al. (2018), *Adversarially Robust Generalization Requires More Data*, arXiv:1804.11285; Soleymani et al. (2026), *Efficient Learning and Symmetry Discovery under Exact Invariances*.

title: Certification for composed semantic transformations
subfield: Robustness, domain shift, and performative effects
open: Certify prediction stability under a specified composition of geometric, photometric, and occlusion transformations with a sound, tractable perturbation model.
status: Research target. Tight Gaussian smoothing certificates for \(\ell_2\) perturbations do not solve semantic-composition certification.
why: Pixel-norm guarantees may not cover the changes users regard as meaning-preserving.
key_works: Cohen, Rosenfeld, and Kolter (2019), *Certified Adversarial Robustness via Randomized Smoothing*, arXiv:1902.02918; Hendrycks and Dietterich (2019), *Benchmarking Neural Network Robustness to Common Corruptions and Perturbations*, arXiv:1903.12261.

title: Worst-group learning with noisy or missing group labels
subfield: Robustness, domain shift, and performative effects
open: Obtain sharp worst-group risk guarantees when group membership is partially observed or noisy and groups overlap.
status: Research target. Group-distributionally robust optimization with known groups supplies a baseline, but group uncertainty changes identifiability and sample requirements.
why: The vulnerable groups an application should protect may not be cleanly annotated.
key_works: Sagawa et al. (2020), *Distributionally Robust Neural Networks for Group Shifts*, arXiv:1911.08731; Koh et al. (2021), *WILDS*, arXiv:2012.07421.

title: Finite-environment guarantees for domain generalization
subfield: Robustness, domain shift, and performative effects
open: Determine the number and diversity of training environments needed to guarantee performance on a specified meta-distribution of unseen environments.
status: Research target. Arbitrary unseen-distribution guarantees are impossible without assumptions; existing empirical protocols do not determine the right environment-complexity measure.
why: More examples from one environment may not substitute for observing more environments.
key_works: Gulrajani and Lopez-Paz (2021), *In Search of Lost Domain Generalization*, arXiv:2007.01434; Arjovsky et al. (2019), *Invariant Risk Minimization*, arXiv:1907.02893.

title: Testable out-of-distribution detection guarantees
subfield: Robustness, domain shift, and performative effects
open: Characterize restricted shift families for which one can test deployment assumptions and guarantee a useful false-alarm versus missed-shift tradeoff.
status: Research target. Detecting every possible unseen distribution is not a meaningful unrestricted guarantee.
why: It would make abstention and monitoring guarantees conditional on explicit, inspectable assumptions.
key_works: Koh et al. (2021), *WILDS*, arXiv:2012.07421; Goel et al. (2026), *Testing Noise Assumptions of Learning Algorithms*.

title: Learning performative optima rather than stable fixed points
subfield: Robustness, domain shift, and performative effects
open: Learn a globally good performative decision when deploying the predictor changes the data distribution, without confusing distributional stability with optimality.
status: Performative prediction has supplied convergence results under structural conditions since 2020. General global optimization under unknown response dynamics remains a target.
why: A system can stabilize at a self-confirming but socially or operationally poor outcome.
key_works: Perdomo, Zrnic, Mendler-Dünner, and Hardt (2020), *Performative Prediction*, arXiv:2002.06673.

title: Multi-agent performative learning
subfield: Robustness, domain shift, and performative effects
open: Characterize convergence, welfare, and learnability when several independently adapting predictors jointly change the population they observe.
status: Research target. Single-deployer stability assumptions do not generally survive interacting strategic learners.
why: Markets, recommendation ecosystems, and competing platforms contain multiple adaptive decision-makers.
key_works: Perdomo et al. (2020), arXiv:2002.06673; Foster et al. (2023), *On the Complexity of Multi-Agent Decision Making*, arXiv:2305.00684.

title: Sharp conditional coverage under explicit regularity
open: Under a stated smoothness or low-complexity conditional model, determine the optimal tradeoff between local coverage accuracy and prediction-set size.
status: Exact nontrivial distribution-free conditional coverage is already impossible. The open target is a sharp restricted-model frontier.
why: Marginal coverage can conceal severe errors for particular inputs or populations.
key_works: Barber, Candès, Ramdas, and Tibshirani (2020), *The Limits of Distribution-Free Conditional Predictive Inference*, arXiv:1903.04684.

title: Finite-window adaptive coverage with efficient sets
open: Simultaneously control coverage on short windows and prediction-set size under a quantified drift budget, with matching lower bounds.
status: Long-run adaptive coverage methods exist. Long-run average validity alone does not guarantee useful coverage during a particular deployment interval.
why: A prediction system can compensate for a dangerous failure period with later overcoverage.
key_works: Gibbs and Candès (2021), *Adaptive Conformal Inference Under Distribution Shift*, arXiv:2106.00170; Barber et al. (2023), *Conformal Prediction Beyond Exchangeability*, arXiv:2202.13415.

title: Optimal conformal inference with estimated density ratios
open: Obtain sharp coverage and efficiency guarantees when covariate-shift weights are estimated from finite data and may be misspecified.
status: Weighted conformal prediction under covariate shift is established; estimated-ratio error must be accounted for rather than treated as known.
why: Exact deployment-to-training density ratios are almost never available.
key_works: Tibshirani, Barber, Candès, and Ramdas (2019), *Conformal Prediction Under Covariate Shift*, arXiv:1904.06019.

title: Efficient rich-group conditional guarantees
open: Achieve computationally and statistically efficient coverage over a rich, overlapping family of groups, including groups selected after inspecting previous outputs.
status: Conditional guarantees for specified finite-dimensional shift families are known. Rich and adaptively chosen families impose additional statistical and computational costs.
why: It would make uncertainty guarantees meaningful for intersectional and discovered subpopulations.
key_works: Gibbs, Cherian, and Candès (2024), *Conformal Prediction With Conditional Guarantees*, arXiv:2305.12616; Hébert-Johnson et al. (2018), arXiv:1711.08513.

title: Risk control for variable-length generated outputs
open: Construct practically sized sets or abstention policies for variable-length generated outputs that control a specified semantic loss, including the uncertainty of the loss evaluator.
status: Research target. Conformal risk control supplies a general framework, but semantic evaluation and enormous output spaces create additional unresolved requirements.
why: It would extend uncertainty guarantees beyond fixed-label classification.
key_works: Angelopoulos et al. (2024), *Conformal Risk Control*, arXiv:2208.02814.

title: Unknown-dependence conformal prediction
open: Adapt prediction intervals to unknown temporal dependence while retaining sharp finite-sample validity and avoiding excessively conservative widths.
status: Beyond-exchangeability methods quantify departures from ideal assumptions; adaptation to unknown dependence strength remains a separate target.
why: Sequential observations often have dependence that changes over time.
key_works: Barber et al. (2023), *Conformal Prediction Beyond Exchangeability*, arXiv:2202.13415; Howard et al. (2021), *Time-Uniform, Nonparametric, Nonasymptotic Confidence Sequences*, arXiv:1810.08240.

title: Selective uncertainty after adaptive model comparison
open: Preserve useful prediction guarantees when users repeatedly compare, filter, and select models or prediction sets using the same calibration information.
status: Research target. Validity of one prespecified conformal procedure does not automatically survive unrestricted adaptive selection.
why: Deployment workflows commonly choose the narrowest-looking or best-performing uncertainty method after inspection.
key_works: Dwork et al. (2015), arXiv:1506.02629; Angelopoulos et al. (2024), *Conformal Risk Control*, arXiv:2208.02814.

title: Uncertainty decomposition that is empirically identifiable
open: Under a specified model family and repeated-data protocol, identify which components of predictive uncertainty can be separated into irreducible noise, finite-data uncertainty, and model misspecification.
status: Proposed target. Naming uncertainty components does not establish that they are identifiable from one trained model’s outputs.
why: Different uncertainty sources call for different interventions: more data, a different model, or acceptance of irreducible ambiguity.
key_works: Barber et al. (2020), arXiv:1903.04684; Watanabe (2013), *A Widely Applicable Bayesian Information Criterion*.

title: How much harder is approximately private PAC learning?
open: Determine whether approximately differentially private learning of finite concept classes can require a large gap above nonprivate VC-based sample complexity, beyond presently understood separations.
status: Explicit COLT 2026 question. Approximate-DP learnability and online learnability coincide qualitatively, but that does not settle the finite-class quantitative gap.
why: It asks whether privacy’s worst-case statistical price is fundamentally modest or very large.
key_works: Nissim, Stemmer, and Tsfadia (2026), *Invited Open Problem: Does Differential Privacy Make PAC Learning Much Harder?*

title: Optimal private stochastic expert-learning rates
open: Determine matching rates for stochastic decision-theoretic online learning under differential privacy, with explicit dependence on expert complexity, privacy, and stochastic difficulty.
status: Explicit COLT 2024 problem.
why: It would clarify the cost of learning from sensitive feedback over time.
key_works: Hu and Mehta (2024), *Open Problem: Optimal Rates for Stochastic Decision-Theoretic Online Learning Under Differentially Privacy*.

title: Computationally useful private learning under distributional restrictions
open: Turn distribution-restricted private-learnability characterizations into efficient algorithms with sharp sample and runtime dependence on the restriction parameters.
status: Research target. Generalized-smoothness characterizations appeared in 2026; qualitative characterization is not the same as an efficient implementation for an implicit class.
why: Practical data assumptions may make privacy much cheaper than worst-case theory predicts.
key_works: Blanchard, Shetty, and Rakhlin (2026), *Characterizing Online and Private Learnability under Distributional Constraints via Generalized Smoothness*.

title: Exact large-model unlearning substantially faster than retraining
open: For a specified training algorithm and deletion regime, produce the same output distribution as retraining without deleted data while reducing total deletion-handling computation by at least an order of magnitude.
status: Proposed moonshot. Partitioned retraining and certified approximate deletion methods exist; the exact, large-model, broad-deletion target is stronger.
why: It would make deletion guarantees operational rather than prohibitively expensive.
key_works: Bourtoule et al. (2021), *Machine Unlearning*, arXiv:1912.03817; Neel, Roth, and Sharifi-Malvajerdi (2021), *Descent-to-Delete*, arXiv:2007.02923.

title: Optimal deletion-capacity tradeoffs
open: Determine matching accuracy, memory, update-time, and deletion-capacity bounds for repeated unlearning under adaptive deletion requests.
status: Research target. Existing unlearning theory provides important tradeoffs, but the full adaptive resource frontier depends on training and storage constraints.
why: Supporting one deletion is different from supporting a long sequence of deletions economically.
key_works: Sekhari et al. (2021), *Remember What You Want to Forget: Algorithms for Machine Unlearning*, arXiv:2103.03279; Neel et al. (2021), arXiv:2007.02923.

title: Unlearning through derived models and artifacts
open: Define and enforce deletion guarantees across finetuned descendants, distilled models, cached embeddings, and other artifacts derived from an affected model.
status: Proposed target. A guarantee for one model state does not automatically remove information from its descendants.
why: Modern training systems form dependency graphs rather than isolated model files.
key_works: Bourtoule et al. (2021), *Machine Unlearning*, arXiv:1912.03817; Sekhari et al. (2021), arXiv:2103.03279.

title: Auditable certificates of unlearning
open: Construct independently checkable certificates that a deletion procedure meets a formally specified retraining-equivalence or approximate-unlearning guarantee.
status: Proposed target. Failure of a membership-inference attack is not itself proof that unlearning succeeded.
why: It would permit third-party verification without rerunning the entire original training procedure.
key_works: Neel et al. (2021), *Descent-to-Delete*, arXiv:2007.02923; Sekhari et al. (2021), arXiv:2103.03279.

title: Private learning with rare, changing user groups
open: Achieve useful user-level privacy and worst-group accuracy when participation rates and group prevalence change, with sharp dependence on the smallest supported groups.
status: Research target combining privacy, heterogeneous participation, and group-robust learning.
why: Average privacy-preserving accuracy can conceal failure for infrequent users or small populations.
key_works: Kairouz et al. (2021), *Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning*, arXiv:1912.04977; Sagawa et al. (2020), arXiv:1911.08731.

title: Numerically faithful privacy guarantees
open: Build an end-to-end accounting and implementation framework proving that finite-precision randomness, clipping, aggregation, and adaptive training preserve the claimed privacy parameters.
status: Proposed infrastructure target. Mathematical privacy analysis and a concrete numerical implementation are separate objects requiring a verified connection.
why: A privacy theorem is not sufficient when the implemented random mechanism differs from the analyzed one.
key_works: Kairouz et al. (2021), *Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning*, arXiv:1912.04977.

title: Joint privacy–unlearning optimality
open: Characterize when adding privacy during training reduces future deletion cost optimally, and when stronger privacy merely sacrifices accuracy without meaningful unlearning benefit.
status: Research target. Differential privacy and unlearning are related but impose different operational requirements.
why: It would help choose between paying an upfront privacy cost and maintaining expensive deletion infrastructure.
key_works: Sekhari et al. (2021), *Remember What You Want to Forget*, arXiv:2103.03279; Nissim et al. (2026), *Does Differential Privacy Make PAC Learning Much Harder?*

title: Computational cost of replicable learning
open: Characterize which efficiently learnable classes also admit efficient replicable learners, with sharp dependence on replication probability and accuracy.
status: Replicability became a formal learning-theoretic program in 2022. Statistical existence need not imply an efficient reproducible algorithm.
why: Two independent datasets should sometimes support the same operational decision, not merely similar average risk.
key_works: Impagliazzo, Lei, Pitassi, and Sorrell (2022), *Reproducibility in Learning*, arXiv:2201.08430.

title: Sharp conversions between privacy, stability, and replicability
open: Determine optimal parameter losses when converting among private, stable, and replicable learners for explicit problem families.
status: Research target. Connections exist, but the properties are not interchangeable at identical sample and computational cost.
why: It would reveal whether one training mechanism can deliver several reliability guarantees efficiently.
key_works: Impagliazzo et al. (2022), *Reproducibility in Learning*, arXiv:2201.08430; Nissim et al. (2026), *Does Differential Privacy Make PAC Learning Much Harder?*

title: Replicability under adaptive composition
open: Guarantee replication of an entire adaptively chosen sequence of learning and decision steps, rather than one isolated estimator.
status: Research target. Errors and data dependence can compound when replicated components are assembled into a workflow.
why: Scientific and industrial pipelines make many contingent decisions after inspecting intermediate results.
key_works: Impagliazzo et al. (2022), arXiv:2201.08430; Dwork et al. (2015), arXiv:1506.02629.

title: Reusable evaluation under a changing population
open: Control adaptive evaluation error when a benchmark is repeatedly queried while the deployment population itself changes.
status: Research target. Reusable-holdout methods address adaptivity; distribution-shift methods address drift. Their joint sharp treatment requires both.
why: A benchmark can remain statistically protected against overuse yet become irrelevant to current deployment.
key_works: Dwork et al. (2015), *Generalization in Adaptive Data Analysis and Holdout Reuse*, arXiv:1506.02629; Barber et al. (2023), arXiv:2202.13415.

title: Counterexample generation for theorem assumptions
open: Build a system that takes a learning theorem’s formal assumptions and generates small counterexamples when a claimed application violates a necessary condition.
status: Proposed infrastructure target. Existing theory supplies many isolated impossibility constructions, but not a standardized assumption-to-counterexample workflow.
why: It would reduce misapplication of theorems to incompatible data, access models, or computational regimes.
key_works: Goel et al. (2026), *Testing Noise Assumptions of Learning Algorithms*; Nagarajan and Kolter (2019), arXiv:1902.04742.

title: Machine-checkable learning-theory benchmark claims
open: Produce a benchmark format in which theorem assumptions, algorithm versions, numerical experiments, and claimed rate comparisons can be independently replayed and checked.
status: Proposed infrastructure target; no claim is made that existing theorem provers or reproducibility initiatives are absent.
why: It would expose mismatches between asymptotic claims, implemented algorithms, and empirical evidence.
key_works: Impagliazzo et al. (2022), *Reproducibility in Learning*, arXiv:2201.08430; Berner et al. (2021), *The Modern Mathematics of Deep Learning*, arXiv:2105.04026.

title: Is interaction necessary for optimal one-bit mean estimation?
open: Can arbitrary nonadaptive one-bit quantizers attain order-optimal mean-estimation rates over the specified finite-moment distribution classes, or is interaction necessary?
status: Explicit COLT 2026 problem. Adaptive and two-stage protocols attain optimal rates; nonadaptive threshold and interval schemes can be suboptimal.
why: It isolates the statistical value of feedback when each observation contributes only one bit.
key_works: Lau and Scarlett (2026), *Open Problem: Is Interaction Necessary for Order-Optimal 1-bit Mean Estimation?*

title: Learning under informative client availability
open: Identify and correct participation bias when client availability depends on private data or current model behavior, under explicit identifiability assumptions.
status: Research target. Standard heterogeneous-data analyses do not automatically cover missing-not-at-random participation.
why: A federated model can systematically underlearn from users who rarely participate.
key_works: Kairouz et al. (2021), *Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning*, arXiv:1912.04977; McMahan et al. (2017), *Communication-Efficient Learning of Deep Networks from Decentralized Data*, arXiv:1602.05629.

title: Instance-optimal federated personalization
open: Attain the best tradeoff between shared and client-specific estimation without knowing the degree or structure of heterogeneity in advance.
status: Research target. Heterogeneity-correction methods provide important guarantees but do not determine a universal instance-optimal personalization rule.
why: Excessive sharing harms unusual clients, while excessive personalization wastes common information.
key_works: Karimireddy et al. (2020), *SCAFFOLD: Stochastic Controlled Averaging for Federated Learning*, arXiv:1910.06378; Kairouz et al. (2021), arXiv:1912.04977.

title: Privacy, secure aggregation, and Byzantine robustness together
open: Determine sharp accuracy and breakdown guarantees when the server sees only secure aggregates, some clients are malicious, and honest clients require user-level privacy.
status: Research target. Guarantees proved with individually inspectable updates do not automatically survive secure aggregation.
why: Privacy mechanisms can remove exactly the information a robust aggregator needs.
key_works: Kairouz et al. (2021), *Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning*, arXiv:1912.04977.

title: Total-bit complexity of heterogeneous stochastic optimization
open: Derive matching bounds counting all transmitted bits, communication rounds, local computation, and final statistical error under heterogeneous client objectives.
status: Research target. Round complexity alone can hide large messages or excessive local work.
why: It would make communication-efficiency claims comparable across distributed algorithms.
key_works: McMahan et al. (2017), arXiv:1602.05629; Karimireddy et al. (2020), *SCAFFOLD*, arXiv:1910.06378.

title: Adaptive communication without oracle heterogeneity parameters
open: Choose local-update counts, synchronization frequency, and quantization levels online while matching the best fixed policy chosen with knowledge of the data heterogeneity.
status: Research target. Static tuning can require the very heterogeneity information distributed learning is trying to discover.
why: It would reduce communication without causing uncontrolled client drift.
key_works: Karimireddy et al. (2020), *SCAFFOLD*, arXiv:1910.06378; McMahan et al. (2017), arXiv:1602.05629.

title: Task-aware limits of oversquashing repair
open: Determine the minimum architectural or graph-rewiring resources needed to preserve information relevant to a specified long-range graph task.
status: Oversquashing and message-passing bottlenecks are established; a universal rewiring heuristic is not a task-specific optimality theorem.
why: It would distinguish useful connectivity changes from expensive modifications that destroy relevant graph semantics.
key_works: Alon and Yahav (2021), *On the Bottleneck of Graph Neural Networks and Its Practical Implications*, arXiv:2006.05205.

title: Statistical efficiency of higher-order graph expressivity
open: Quantify when increasing a graph network’s expressivity beyond ordinary message passing improves learnable risk enough to justify its sample and computational cost.
status: Expressivity hierarchies are well developed; representational distinctions alone do not settle statistical or optimization benefits.
why: More expressive graph models can be substantially more expensive without improving the task.
key_works: Xu, Hu, Leskovec, and Jegelka (2019), *How Powerful Are Graph Neural Networks?*, arXiv:1810.00826.

title: Provable optimization for graph algorithm extrapolation
open: Prove that practical training reaches the structured solutions required for algorithmic graph extrapolation, rather than assuming the regularized objective has already been minimized.
status: A 2026 shortest-path result proves that suitably minimized sparse objectives implement Bellman–Ford steps; optimization is a distinct remaining requirement.
why: A representation-and-generalization theorem is incomplete as a training guarantee without reaching its premise.
key_works: Nerem, Chen, Dasgupta, and Wang (2026), *Graph Neural Networks Extrapolate Out-of-Distribution for Shortest Paths*.

title: Size extrapolation for graph algorithms beyond shortest paths
open: Establish trainable architectures with certified size extrapolation for another precisely specified graph algorithm, including its approximation or computational limits.
status: Research target following the 2026 shortest-path result; that theorem does not cover arbitrary graph algorithms.
why: It would reveal whether neural algorithmic alignment generalizes beyond especially favorable dynamic programs.
key_works: Nerem et al. (2026), *Graph Neural Networks Extrapolate Out-of-Distribution for Shortest Paths*; Xu et al. (2019), arXiv:1810.00826.

title: Unknown continuous symmetry discovery
open: Learn a useful unknown continuous symmetry group from data, with computational and statistical guarantees beyond the finite-group subgroup-lattice setting.
status: Known-group invariance, including infinite groups, received polynomial-time results in 2026; unknown finite-group discovery is also addressed. Unknown continuous-group discovery is a different target.
why: Scientific data often contain unknown rotations, scalings, or continuous conservation symmetries.
key_works: Soleymani et al. (2026), *Efficient Learning and Symmetry Discovery under Exact Invariances*.

title: End-to-end mesh-independent operator learning
subfield: Scientific machine learning and operator learning
open: Prove a complete training-to-deployment guarantee whose error and computational accounting remain controlled when evaluation resolution changes.
status: Neural-operator approximation frameworks exist; discretization-invariant architecture alone is not an end-to-end mesh-independent learning theorem.
why: Scientific models should not silently fail when a simulation grid is refined.
key_works: Kovachki et al. (2023), *Neural Operator: Learning Maps Between Function Spaces*, arXiv:2108.08481; Lu et al. (2019 preprint), *DeepONet*, arXiv:1910.03193.

title: Long-horizon statistical accuracy for learned chaotic dynamics
subfield: Scientific machine learning and operator learning
open: Guarantee invariant-measure or long-time observable accuracy for learned chaotic systems without demanding impossible indefinite pointwise trajectory agreement.
status: Research target. Short-horizon prediction error does not automatically control long-run statistical behavior.
why: Climate, fluid, and many-body applications often care about long-term statistics rather than exact trajectories.
key_works: Kovachki et al. (2023), *Neural Operator*, arXiv:2108.08481; Lu et al., *DeepONet*, arXiv:1910.03193.

title: Identifiable operator discovery with unknown forcing
subfield: Scientific machine learning and operator learning
open: Determine which differential operators can be identified from finite noisy trajectories when forcing, boundary conditions, or latent state variables are only partially observed.
status: Research target. Accurately fitting observed trajectories does not uniquely identify the governing operator.
why: It would separate scientific discovery from flexible interpolation of measurements.
key_works: Lu et al., *DeepONet: Learning Nonlinear Operators for Identifying Differential Equations*, arXiv:1910.03193; Kovachki et al. (2023), arXiv:2108.08481.

title: Certified global residual control from sampled physics constraints
subfield: Scientific machine learning and operator learning
open: Turn finite sampled residual checks into rigorous global solution-error certificates for a specified PDE class and neural approximation family.
status: Proposed target. Small residuals at collocation points do not alone certify small error over the entire domain.
why: It would make physics-constrained learning auditable for scientific use.
key_works: Berner et al. (2021), *The Modern Mathematics of Deep Learning*, arXiv:2105.04026; Kovachki et al. (2023), *Neural Operator*, arXiv:2108.08481.

title: Instance-optimal shadow tomography outside the high-precision regime
open: Extend sharp instance-dependent few-copy shadow-tomography guarantees beyond the regime where accuracy lies below the thresholds required by local metrological analysis.
status: A 2026 result characterizes high-precision sample complexity through inverse Fisher information, up to logarithmic factors.
why: It would cover the moderate-accuracy regime relevant to many experiments.
key_works: Chen, Gong, and Zhou (2026), *Instance-Optimal High-Precision Shadow Tomography with Few-Copy Measurements: A Metrological Approach*.

title: Efficient proper learning of structured quantum states
open: Identify broad physically meaningful quantum-state families that admit both sample-efficient prediction and computationally efficient reconstruction within the same family.
status: PAC learnability of quantum states is established in an appropriate predictive sense. Proper, computationally efficient reconstruction is a stronger requirement.
why: Prediction alone may not yield a usable state description for simulation or control.
key_works: Aaronson (2007), *The Learnability of Quantum States*, arXiv:quant-ph/0608142, DOI:10.1098/rspa.2007.0113; Huang, Kueng, and Preskill (2020), arXiv:2002.08953.

title: End-to-end quantum learning advantage on natural data
open: Demonstrate a reproducible learning advantage on a naturally motivated task after charging data access, state preparation, measurement, classical preprocessing, and error correction.
status: Rigorous supervised quantum separations exist, but they do not automatically establish practical end-to-end advantage under realistic access costs.
why: It would distinguish algorithmic speedup from moving costs into the input model.
key_works: Liu, Arunachalam, and Temme (2021), *A Rigorous and Robust Quantum Speed-up in Supervised Machine Learning*, arXiv:2010.02174; Huang et al. (2021), *Power of Data in Quantum Machine Learning*, arXiv:2011.01938.

title: Expressive, trainable, noise-tolerant quantum models
open: Exhibit a quantum-model family simultaneously avoiding barren plateaus, retaining meaningful classical hardness, and learning efficiently under realistic noise.
status: Barren plateaus are established for important random-circuit regimes; avoiding one obstruction alone does not establish the full conjunction.
why: It would reconcile the properties needed for a useful variational quantum learner.
key_works: McClean et al. (2018), *Barren Plateaus in Quantum Neural Network Training Landscapes*, arXiv:1803.11173; Huang et al. (2021), arXiv:2011.01938.

title: Beyond low-degree quantum-learning hardness
open: Strengthen quantum low-degree barriers to broader computational hardness statements for specific state-learning and error-mitigation tasks.
status: A 2026 framework establishes new low-degree information–computation gaps, including adaptive measurement settings; these remain model-specific lower bounds.
why: It would determine whether currently hard quantum inference tasks are fundamentally hard or merely defeat known estimators.
key_works: Chen, Gong, Haferkamp, and Quek (2026), *Information-Computation Gaps in Quantum Learning via Low-Degree Likelihood*.

title: Efficiently implementing instance-optimal quantum measurements
open: Compute and physically implement near-optimal measurement designs for a given observable family without an optimization or circuit cost that overwhelms the sample savings.
status: Research target. An information-theoretic formula involving Fisher information does not automatically provide efficient measurement synthesis.
why: It would convert sample-optimal quantum-learning theory into experimentally usable protocols.
key_works: Chen, Gong, and Zhou (2026), *Instance-Optimal High-Precision Shadow Tomography*; Huang, Kueng, and Preskill (2020), *Predicting Many Properties of a Quantum System from Very Few Measurements*, arXiv:2002.08953.

title: Generalization-theory falsification corpus
open: Create a benchmark of matched training runs that systematically vary labels, parameterization, optimization, and data structure while holding competing complexity measures constant where possible.
status: Proposed dataset target. Existing counterexamples and empirical studies provide components, not the complete controlled corpus specified here.
why: It would let theories make discriminating predictions instead of merely correlating with a small set of successful runs.
key_works: Zhang et al. (2017), arXiv:1611.03530; Nagarajan and Kolter (2019), arXiv:1902.04742.

title: Joint neural scaling phase-diagram measurements
open: Measure training behavior over a preregistered grid of width, depth, sample size, batch size, and learning rate, with replicated seeds and complete trajectories.
status: Proposed dataset target. Separate width limits or scaling-law fits do not substitute for the joint intervention grid.
why: It would expose interactions hidden by one-variable-at-a-time scaling studies.
key_works: Yang et al. (2022), *Tensor Programs V*, arXiv:2203.03466; Cohen et al. (2021), *Edge of Stability*, arXiv:2103.00065.

title: Causal benchmark for in-context algorithm identification
open: Build tasks where candidate internal algorithms make different predictions under carefully chosen prompt interventions, and evaluate identification rather than ordinary task accuracy.
status: Proposed benchmark target building on linear-model and mechanistic studies.
why: Similar outputs on standard prompts do not identify which learning algorithm a model implements.
key_works: Akyürek et al. (2023), *What Learning Algorithm Is In-Context Learning?*, arXiv:2211.15661; Garg et al. (2022), arXiv:2208.01066.

title: Distribution shifts with documented generating mechanisms
open: Assemble a benchmark whose shifts have recorded causal mechanisms, intervention metadata, and stable task definitions, enabling tests of specific shift theories.
status: Proposed extension beyond ordinary shift benchmarks; WILDS already supplies important real-world shift datasets.
why: A performance drop alone does not reveal which distributional assumption failed.
key_works: Koh et al. (2021), *WILDS: A Benchmark of in-the-Wild Distribution Shifts*, arXiv:2012.07421; Peters et al. (2016), arXiv:1501.01332.

title: Ground-truth memorization and rule-learning benchmark
open: Construct tasks with separately controllable memorization and algorithmic solutions, publish training checkpoints, and measure which solution is causally used.
status: Proposed benchmark target. Grokking datasets provide a starting point but not a comprehensive ground-truth mechanism census.
why: It would test claims about compression, generalization, and reasoning against known alternatives.
key_works: Power et al. (2022), *Grokking*, arXiv:2201.02177; Nanda et al. (2023), arXiv:2301.05217.

title: Federated participation and heterogeneity traces
open: Release privacy-preserving datasets recording realistic client availability, local distributions, drift, and communication constraints with enough ground truth to test selection-bias corrections.
status: Proposed data target; existing federated benchmarks do not automatically meet this joint specification.
why: Simulated independent participation can hide the failures most relevant to actual deployments.
key_works: Kairouz et al. (2021), *Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning*, arXiv:1912.04977; McMahan et al. (2017), arXiv:1602.05629.

title: End-to-end energy measurements for learning claims
open: Standardize measurements counting data preparation, tuning, failed runs, training, inference, and verification when comparing algorithms at matched statistical quality.
status: Proposed measurement target. A reduction in nominal training operations is not automatically a reduction in total energy.
why: It would make “10× cheaper” or “100× more efficient” claims scientifically comparable.
key_works: Hoffmann et al. (2022), arXiv:2203.15556; Yang et al. (2022), *Tensor Programs V*, arXiv:2203.03466.

title: Offline-decision benchmarks with hidden oracle separation
open: Build sequential-decision benchmarks that preserve realistic logs while separately maintaining evaluation-only counterfactual information, with auditable prevention of oracle leakage.
status: Proposed benchmark target. A simulator’s full state or reward oracle can silently give a learner stronger access than an offline theorem permits.
why: It would make comparisons between offline-RL theory and experiments valid.
key_works: Levine et al. (2020), *Offline Reinforcement Learning*, arXiv:2005.01643; Tkachuk et al. (2026), *Trajectory Data Suffices…*.

title: Versioned, machine-readable open-problem dependency graph
open: Build a maintained registry that represents precise assumptions, equivalence claims, partial results, superseded formulations, and resolution evidence for learning-theory problems.
status: Proposed infrastructure target. Conference open-problem papers exist; the requested cross-linked, version-aware census is a stronger artifact.
why: It would prevent repeated work on solved formulations and enable systematic discovery of neighboring unsolved cases.
key_works: Hanneke et al. (2024), *Direct Sums in Learning Theory*; More et al. (2026), *A Rate Separation for Agnostic Direct Sums*, arXiv:2608.06951; COLT 2026 open-problem proceedings.

title: Executable assumption contracts for learning algorithms
open: Package algorithms with machine-readable assumptions, testable checks where possible, and explicit declarations for assumptions that cannot be checked from the available data.
status: Proposed infrastructure target grounded in emerging testable-learning results.
why: It would expose hidden changes in noise, access model, distribution, or computational budget before a theorem is invoked.
key_works: Goel et al. (2026), *Testing Noise Assumptions of Learning Algorithms*.

title: Tenfold reduction in total hyperparameter-search cost
open: Reduce total tuning computation by at least \(10\times\) across a preregistered model-and-task suite while matching a strong full-scale search baseline within a stated quality tolerance.
status: Proposed moonshot. Zero-shot hyperparameter transfer offers a concrete starting mechanism, but the target includes failures, pilot runs, and transfer overhead.
why: Tuning can consume resources comparable to or greater than the final training run.
key_works: Yang et al. (2022), *Tensor Programs V: Tuning Large Neural Networks via Zero-Shot Hyperparameter Transfer*, arXiv:2203.03466.

title: Hundredfold energy reduction with a matched statistical guarantee
open: For a clearly specified learning family, achieve \(100\times\) lower measured lifecycle energy while preserving the same risk target, confidence level, and deployment workload.
status: Proposed moonshot, not a claim that such a factor is universally possible. A solution must identify the exploitable structure and count all displaced costs.
why: It would establish a real algorithmic efficiency breakthrough rather than a hardware or accounting substitution.
key_works: Hoffmann et al. (2022), *Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models*, arXiv:2203.15556; McMahan et al. (2017), arXiv:1602.05629.

title: Tenfold data reduction through verified learned structure
open: Demonstrate a \(10\times\) reduction in independently acquired labeled data using learned invariances or representations, with no privileged task information and matched end-to-end risk.
status: Proposed target. Existing representation and invariance theories motivate the mechanism; the measurement must count data used to discover the structure.
why: It would quantify genuine learning-to-learn gains rather than moving supervision into pretraining or benchmark design.
key_works: HaoChen et al. (2021), arXiv:2106.04156; Soleymani et al. (2026), *Efficient Learning and Symmetry Discovery under Exact Invariances*.

title: Independent longitudinal compute for theory-discriminating experiments
open: Establish sustained funding and access for replicated, preregistered training experiments that compare competing theories over multiple scales and publish unsuccessful runs.
status: Proposed funding target. Programs such as the US National AI Research Resource already expand access; the gap specified here is durable support for this particular longitudinal experimental mandate.
why: Some theories cannot be discriminated using small, one-off runs, and commercial release incentives need not support negative results.
key_works: US National Science Foundation, *National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource*, current program description; Kaplan et al. (2020), *Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models*, arXiv:2001.08361.

title: Funded maintenance of negative results and benchmark validity
open: Create a durable funding and governance mechanism for maintaining theorem-status registries, replication artifacts, counterexamples, and benchmark contamination records after their original publication.
status: Proposed funding target. The requirement is ongoing maintenance with explicit service obligations, not merely launching another repository.
why: A census becomes misleading if solved problems, invalid comparisons, and broken artifacts remain uncorrected.
key_works: Impagliazzo et al. (2022), *Reproducibility in Learning*, arXiv:2201.08430; NSF, *National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource*.

title: Learning a defensible individual-fairness metric
open: Under explicit normative constraints and available comparison data, learn a task-specific similarity metric with identifiable meaning and generalization guarantees.
status: The individual-fairness framework assumes a task-relevant metric; deriving and validating that metric is a separate research problem.
why: “Treat similar people similarly” is operational only when similarity is justified rather than silently chosen.
key_works: Dwork, Hardt, Pitassi, Reingold, and Zemel (2012), *Fairness Through Awareness*, arXiv:1104.3913.

title: Fairness frontiers with selectively observed outcomes
open: Characterize achievable fairness and predictive utility when labels are observed only for people selected by previous policies, including the minimum exploration needed to identify the frontier.
status: Research target. Static postprocessing guarantees with fully observed outcomes do not resolve selective-label feedback.
why: Historical decisions determine which outcomes become available for learning.
key_works: Hardt, Price, and Srebro (2016), *Equality of Opportunity in Supervised Learning*, arXiv:1610.02413; Liu et al. (2018), *Delayed Impact of Fair Machine Learning*, arXiv:1803.04383.

title: Long-run welfare guarantees for adaptive fair policies
open: Learn policies that satisfy explicitly chosen long-run welfare constraints when decisions change future group distributions and the transition model is initially unknown.
status: One-step delayed-impact models already show that static fairness criteria can harm intended beneficiaries. Multi-step learning with welfare guarantees is a stronger target.
why: Short-run parity is not a substitute for understanding long-run effects.
key_works: Liu, Dean, Rolf, Simchowitz, and Hardt (2018), *Delayed Impact of Fair Machine Learning*, arXiv:1803.04383; Perdomo et al. (2020), arXiv:2002.06673.

title: Multicalibration under endogenous outcomes
open: Maintain useful subgroup calibration when deploying predictions changes outcomes and group membership, with explicit bounds on feedback-induced calibration failure.
status: Research target combining multicalibration with performative prediction; static calibration need not be preserved after intervention.
why: A forecast used to allocate resources can alter the event it was calibrated to predict.
key_works: Hébert-Johnson, Kim, Reingold, and Rothblum (2018), *Calibration for the Computationally-Identifiable Masses*, arXiv:1711.08513; Perdomo et al. (2020), *Performative Prediction*, arXiv:2002.06673.

title: Computing learning coefficients for deep singular models
open: Compute or sharply bound the real log canonical threshold and related learning coefficients for specified deep-network families with nonidentifiable parameters.
status: Singular learning theory explains why ordinary parameter counting fails, but obtaining explicit coefficients for complex architectures remains a substantial target.
why: These quantities govern asymptotic evidence and generalization behavior in singular models.
key_works: Watanabe (2013), *A Widely Applicable Bayesian Information Criterion*, JMLR 14:867–897; Watanabe (2010), *Asymptotic Equivalence of Bayes Cross Validation and Widely Applicable Information Criterion in Singular Learning Theory*.

title: Finite-sample validity of singular-model information criteria
open: Derive explicit finite-sample error bounds for WAIC- or WBIC-style model comparisons when model dimension and architecture complexity grow with sample size.
status: Asymptotic equivalences and singular-model criteria are established; uniform finite-sample accuracy in growing deep models is a separate target.
why: Practical model selection happens at finite sample sizes, often far from fixed-model asymptotics.
key_works: Watanabe (2010), *Asymptotic Equivalence of Bayes Cross Validation and Widely Applicable Information Criterion in Singular Learning Theory*; Watanabe (2013), *A Widely Applicable Bayesian Information Criterion*.

title: Calibrated uncertainty on singular predictor quotients
open: Construct credible regions for identifiable predictive quantities that retain valid uncertainty interpretation despite parameter symmetries and singular posterior geometry.
status: Research target. Parameter-space Gaussian approximations can be inappropriate when many parameters represent the same predictor.
why: It would make Bayesian uncertainty meaningful in overparameterized models without pretending their parameters are identifiable.
key_works: Watanabe (2013), *A Widely Applicable Bayesian Information Criterion*; Tinati and Tu (2026), *On the Asymptotics of Self-Supervised Pre-training*.

title: Singular learning theory with dependent and augmented samples
open: Determine how learning coefficients and predictive-risk expansions change when observations are dependent or generated through augmentation of a smaller underlying sample.
status: Research target. Treating augmented observations as independent can misstate the effective information available to a singular model.
why: It would connect singular asymptotics to modern pretraining and augmentation workflows.
key_works: Watanabe (2010), *Asymptotic Equivalence of Bayes Cross Validation and Widely Applicable Information Criterion in Singular Learning Theory*; Holzman, Moran, and Shlimovich (2026), *Uniform Laws of Large Numbers in Product Spaces*, arXiv:2603.24493.
